Voluntary acts (nawafil) barely enter into this, because the responsible person does not fear punishment for leaving them; he only hopes for reward for performing them. The second issue: they differed about its time. From ʿAlqamah and al-Shaʿbi: this convulsion will occur in the world, and it is the one accompanied by the rising of the sun from its west. It was said: it is the one that will accompany the Hour. It has been narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), regarding the hadith of the Trumpet: "It is a great horn into which three blasts will be blown: the blast of terror, the blast of swooning, and the blast of rising to the Lord of the worlds. At the blast of terror, Allah will set the mountains in motion, and the quaking one will quake, followed by the follower. 'Hearts that Day will be trembling' [al-Naziʿat, 8], and the earth will be like a ship being tossed by the waves, or like a hanging lamp shaken by the winds." Muqatil and Ibn Zayd said: this is at the beginning of the first day of the Hereafter. Know that the wording gives no indication of any of these divisions, because this idafah (construct phrase) is valid whether the convulsion comes before it and is among its signs and portents, or whether it occurs within it and together with it, as when we say: "the signs of the Hour" and "the portents of the Hour."

The third issue: it has been narrated that these two verses "were revealed at night while the people were traveling. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called out, and the people gathered around him, and he recited them to them. No one was seen weeping more than on that night. When they woke in the morning, they did not unload the saddles, did not pitch the tents, and did not cook in the pots, while the people were between weeping, sitting sorrowful, and deep in thought. He, peace be upon him, said: 'Do you know which day that is?' They said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'That is the Day when Allah says to Adam, peace be upon him: Rise and send forth the company of the Fire from your offspring. Adam will say: What is the company of the Fire? — meaning, how many? — And Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will say: From every thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine to the Fire and one to Paradise. At that time the child will turn gray, and every pregnant woman will drop her load, and you will see people as intoxicated.'" This was hard upon the believers, and they wept and said: "Then who will be saved, O Messenger of Allah?" He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Rejoice, be steadfast, and be moderate, for among you are two creatures who have never been among a people without multiplying them: Yajuj and Majuj." Then he said: "Indeed, I hope that you will be a quarter of the people of Paradise." They exclaimed Allahu akbar. Then he said: "Indeed, I hope that you will be half of the people of Paradise." They exclaimed Allahu akbar and praised Allah. Then he said: "Indeed, I hope that you will be two-thirds of the people of Paradise. The people of Paradise are a hundred and twenty rows, eighty of them from my community. The Muslims among the disbelievers are only like a mole on the flank of a camel, or like a white hair on a black bull." Then he said: "And seventy thousand of my community will enter Paradise without reckoning." ʿUmar said: "Seventy thousand?" He said: "Yes, and with each one of them seventy thousand." Then ʿUkkashah ibn Miḥṣan stood up and said: "O Messenger of Allah, pray to Allah that He makes me one of them." He said: "You are one of them." Then a man from the Ansar stood up and said the same. He said: "ʿUkkashah has preceded you in that." The people then debated about the seventy thousand. Some of them said: "They are those born upon Islam." Others said: "They are those who believed and fought alongside the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." They informed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of what they had said, and he said: "They are those who do not seek cauterization, nor do they cauterize, nor do they seek incantation, nor do they believe in omens, and upon their Lord they rely."

The fourth issue: He, glorified is He, commanded people to have taqwa, then gave as the reason for its obligation upon them the mention of the Hour, and described it with the most frightening description. The meaning is that taqwa requires averting such a great harm from oneself, and averting harm from oneself is known to be obligatory, so it follows that taqwa is obligatory.

* * *

The fifth issue: the Mu'tazilah argued with His words, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing﴾, describing it as "a thing" even though it is non-existent. They also argued with His words, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things competent﴾ [al-Baqarah, 20]. The thing over which Allah has power is either existent or non-existent. The first is impossible, otherwise it would follow that the Capable is capable of bringing into being what already exists. When this is proven false, it is established that the thing over which Allah has power is non-existent, so the non-existent is a thing. They also argued with His words, the Exalted: ﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow"﴾ [al-Kahf, 23]: He applied the name "thing" in the present to what will become an object of action tomorrow, and what will become an object of action tomorrow is non-existent in the present; so the non-existent is a thing. And Allah knows best.

The answer to the first: zalzalah is an expression for moving bodies, and they are substances in which accidents subsist. The realization of that in the non-existent is impossible, so zalzalah cannot be a thing while it does not exist. Therefore there must be an interpretation, by agreement. The meaning is that when it comes into existence it becomes a thing. This is the answer to the rest.

The sixth issue: Allah described the convulsion as "tremendous," and there is nothing more tremendous than what Allah has made tremendous.

* * *

As for His words, the Exalted: ﴿On the Day you see it﴾ [p. 5] — it is in the accusative, governed by ﴿distracted﴾, meaning: they will be distracted on that Day. The pronoun in ﴿you see it﴾ may refer to the convulsion or to the Hour, since both have been mentioned, but the nearer reference is to the convulsion, because witnessing it is what causes intense fear. Know that He, glorified and exalted, mentioned three matters from the terrors of that Day.

The first: His words, ﴿every nursing mother will be distracted from that which she nursed﴾, meaning the convulsion will distract her. Dhuhul is departing from a matter with bewilderment. I say: the mursiḍah is the one who is in the state of nursing, actually giving the child her breast, while murḍiʿ is one whose nature is to nurse even if she is not actually nursing at the time of the description. So He said mursiḍah to indicate that when this terror surprises her while she has put the infant to her breast, she will pull it from her mouth because of the astonishment that overtakes her. His words ﴿from that which she nursed﴾ mean: from her nursing, or from the one she nursed, who is the infant; in this interpretation, "mā" (that which) means "man" (the one who).

The second: His words, ﴿and every pregnant woman will drop her load﴾. The meaning is that she will miscarry her child, whether fully formed or not, from the terror of that Day. This indicates that this convulsion occurs before the resurrection. Al-Hasan said: the nursing mother will be distracted from her child without weaning, and the pregnant women will cast what is in their wombs before full term. al-Qaffal said: it is possible to say that whoever died pregnant or nursing will be resurrected pregnant or nursing, and will drop her load from fear. It is also possible that the meaning of the nursing mother's distraction and the dropping of the load is by way of parable, just as His words were interpreted: ﴿a Day that will make the children gray-haired﴾ [al-Muzzammil, 17].

* * *

The third: His words, ﴿and you will see people as intoxicated﴾. On this there are issues:

The first issue: it was recited "watura" with a damma (ḍamm), meaning: "uriituka qaʾiman" or "raʾaytuka qaʾiman" (I showed you standing / I saw you standing). Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 22, verses 3–4:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And among people is one who disputes about God without knowledge and follows every rebellious devil.﴾ ﴿It has been decreed for him that whoever takes him as an ally, he will lead him astray and guide him to the punishment of the Blaze.﴾ And in this are several issues:

Page 6
The first issue: concerning the manner of the arrangement (nazm, the coherence of the verses), there are two views:

The first: God, exalted is He, previously informed about the terrors of the Day of Resurrection and its severity, and called people to the fear of God. Then in this verse He explained a group of people among those mentioned at the beginning, and informed about their disputation.

The second: that He, exalted is He, explained that alongside this severe warning, through the mention of the convulsion of the Hour and its hardships, there are among people those who dispute about God without knowledge. Then in His saying ﴿And among people﴾ there are two views:

The first: that they are those who deny the resurrection, and this is indicated by His saying ﴿Does not man see that We created him from a drop [of semen]?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 77] to the end of the verse. Also, what precedes this verse is a description of the resurrection, and what follows it is evidence for the resurrection, so it is necessary that the intended dispute here be the dispute concerning the resurrection.

The second: that it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who used to deny the Qur'an and claim that it was "the fables of the ancients," and would say: "What Muhammad brings you is just like what I used to relate to you about the past generations." This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father.

The second issue: this verse, by its implication, indicates the permissibility of sound disputation, because the restriction of disputation to the case of lacking knowledge of the proofs indicates that disputation with knowledge is permissible. Thus, false disputation is what is meant by His saying ﴿They did not present it to you except as a argument.﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 58], and sound disputation is what is meant by His saying ﴿And argue with them in the way that is best.﴾ [An-Nahl: 125].

The third issue: concerning His saying ﴿and follows every rebellious devil﴾ there are two views: one of them is that it may mean the devils of mankind, who are the leaders of the disbelievers who call those beneath them to disbelief; the second is that what is meant is Iblis and his armies. Al-Zajjaj said: al-marid and al-marid mean the elevated and smooth; it is said "a smooth rock" (sakhra marda'), i.e., smooth (mal'a'). It may also be used of other than a devil when he exceeds the limit of his kind.

As for His saying ﴿It has been decreed for him﴾, there are two views:

One of them: that "the writing upon him" is a figure of speech, meaning as if the misguidance of whoever follows him had been written and marked upon him, because this is evident in his condition.

The second: "It has been decreed for him" in the Mother of the Book. Know that this pronoun, after the mention of the one who disputes and after the mention of the devil, may refer to each of them. If it refers to the one who disputes, then it returns to his wording, which is singular, so it is as if He said: it has been decreed upon one who follows the devil that whoever takes the devil as ally, He will mislead him from Paradise and guide him to the Fire. This is a warning from Him, exalted is He, so it is as if He said: it has been decreed upon one of this condition that he will become deserving of this threat. If it refers to the devil, the meaning is: and he follows every rebellious devil, upon whom it has been decreed that whoever accepts from him is in error. On this view too, it is a warning against following him. There are issues in the verse:

The first issue: Qadi 'Abd al-Jabbar said: If it is said that what is meant by His saying ﴿It has been decreed for him﴾ is "it has been decreed upon him," then it cannot be referred except to the one who follows the devil, because God, exalted is He, may not decree upon the devil that he misguides, while He may decree upon the one who accepts from him, by saying: "He has misled him from Paradise and guided him to the Fire." Our companions, may God have mercy on them, said: when that was decreed upon him, if it did not occur, God's true report would turn into a lie, and that is impossible, and what necessitates the impossible is impossible; so its non-occurrence is impossible.

The second issue: the verse indicates that one who disputes about God without knowing the truth is blameworthy and punished, which indicates that knowledge of the truths is not a necessity (darura).

The third issue: the Qadi said: in it is an indication that disputation about God is not from the creation of God, exalted is He, and by His will; otherwise it would not be ascribed to following the devil, and it would not be valid to say that the devil misleads him; rather God, exalted is He, would have misled him.

Page 7
The answer: the counter-argument is the issue of knowledge and the issue of the caller (da'i).

The fourth issue: it is read ﴿annahu﴾ with a fatha and with a kasra. As for the one who reads it with a fatha, it is because the first is the subject of "kutiba" and the second is conjoined to it. As for the one who reads it with a kasra, it is by way of quoting what is written, as it is, as if this statement had been written upon him, just as one says: "I wrote that God is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy"; or on the supposition of "qila" (it was said); or because "kutiba" carries the sense of speech.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 22, verses 3–4:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And among people is one who disputes about God without knowledge and follows every rebellious devil.﴾ ﴿It has been decreed for him that whoever takes him as an ally, he will lead him astray and guide him to the punishment of the Blaze.﴾ And in this are several issues:

Page 6
The first issue: concerning the manner of the arrangement (nazm, the coherence of the verses), there are two views:

The first: God, exalted is He, previously informed about the terrors of the Day of Resurrection and its severity, and called people to the fear of God. Then in this verse He explained a group of people among those mentioned at the beginning, and informed about their disputation.

The second: that He, exalted is He, explained that alongside this severe warning, through the mention of the convulsion of the Hour and its hardships, there are among people those who dispute about God without knowledge. Then in His saying ﴿And among people﴾ there are two views:

The first: that they are those who deny the resurrection, and this is indicated by His saying ﴿Does not man see that We created him from a drop [of semen]?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 77] to the end of the verse. Also, what precedes this verse is a description of the resurrection, and what follows it is evidence for the resurrection, so it is necessary that the intended dispute here be the dispute concerning the resurrection.

The second: that it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who used to deny the Qur'an and claim that it was "the fables of the ancients," and would say: "What Muhammad brings you is just like what I used to relate to you about the past generations." This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father.

The second issue: this verse, by its implication, indicates the permissibility of sound disputation, because the restriction of disputation to the case of lacking knowledge of the proofs indicates that disputation with knowledge is permissible. Thus, false disputation is what is meant by His saying ﴿They did not present it to you except as a argument.﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 58], and sound disputation is what is meant by His saying ﴿And argue with them in the way that is best.﴾ [An-Nahl: 125].

The third issue: concerning His saying ﴿and follows every rebellious devil﴾ there are two views: one of them is that it may mean the devils of mankind, who are the leaders of the disbelievers who call those beneath them to disbelief; the second is that what is meant is Iblis and his armies. Al-Zajjaj said: al-marid and al-marid mean the elevated and smooth; it is said "a smooth rock" (sakhra marda'), i.e., smooth (mal'a'). It may also be used of other than a devil when he exceeds the limit of his kind.

As for His saying ﴿It has been decreed for him﴾, there are two views:

One of them: that "the writing upon him" is a figure of speech, meaning as if the misguidance of whoever follows him had been written and marked upon him, because this is evident in his condition.

The second: "It has been decreed for him" in the Mother of the Book. Know that this pronoun, after the mention of the one who disputes and after the mention of the devil, may refer to each of them. If it refers to the one who disputes, then it returns to his wording, which is singular, so it is as if He said: it has been decreed upon one who follows the devil that whoever takes the devil as ally, He will mislead him from Paradise and guide him to the Fire. This is a warning from Him, exalted is He, so it is as if He said: it has been decreed upon one of this condition that he will become deserving of this threat. If it refers to the devil, the meaning is: and he follows every rebellious devil, upon whom it has been decreed that whoever accepts from him is in error. On this view too, it is a warning against following him. There are issues in the verse:

The first issue: Qadi 'Abd al-Jabbar said: If it is said that what is meant by His saying ﴿It has been decreed for him﴾ is "it has been decreed upon him," then it cannot be referred except to the one who follows the devil, because God, exalted is He, may not decree upon the devil that he misguides, while He may decree upon the one who accepts from him, by saying: "He has misled him from Paradise and guided him to the Fire." Our companions, may God have mercy on them, said: when that was decreed upon him, if it did not occur, God's true report would turn into a lie, and that is impossible, and what necessitates the impossible is impossible; so its non-occurrence is impossible.

The second issue: the verse indicates that one who disputes about God without knowing the truth is blameworthy and punished, which indicates that knowledge of the truths is not a necessity (darura).

The third issue: the Qadi said: in it is an indication that disputation about God is not from the creation of God, exalted is He, and by His will; otherwise it would not be ascribed to following the devil, and it would not be valid to say that the devil misleads him; rather God, exalted is He, would have misled him.

Page 7
The answer: the counter-argument is the issue of knowledge and the issue of the caller (da'i).

The fourth issue: it is read ﴿annahu﴾ with a fatha and with a kasra. As for the one who reads it with a fatha, it is because the first is the subject of "kutiba" and the second is conjoined to it. As for the one who reads it with a kasra, it is by way of quoting what is written, as it is, as if this statement had been written upon him, just as one says: "I wrote that God is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy"; or on the supposition of "qila" (it was said); or because "kutiba" carries the sense of speech.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 22, verse 5:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection, then indeed We created you from dust, then from a drop of semen, then from a clinging clot, then from a lump of flesh, formed and unformed, that We may make clear to you. And We settle in the wombs what We will for an appointed term. Then We bring you out as infants, then [We let you grow] that you may reach your maturity. And among you is he who is taken in death, and among you is he who is returned to the most abject age, so that he knows nothing after having known. And you see the earth lifeless, but when We send down water upon it, it stirs, swells, and sprouts every lovely kind of growth.﴾ ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth, and because He gives life to the dead, and because He is over all things capable.﴾ ﴿And because the Hour is coming, there is no doubt about it, and because Allah will raise those who are in the graves.﴾

**The readings (al-qira'at):** Al-Hasan read ﴿مِنَ البَعَثِ﴾ with the vowel-letter pattern (tahrik), and its parallel is ﴿الحَلَبُ﴾ and ﴿الطَّرَدُ﴾ in ﴿الحَلْبِ﴾ and ﴿الطَّرْدِ﴾. He read ﴿مُخَلَّقَةٍ وغَيْرِ مُخَلَّقَةٍ﴾ with a kasra on the ta' and the ra'. Ibn Abi ʿAbla read both with a fatha. The well-known reading has nūn in ﴿لِنُبَيِّنَ﴾, in ﴿ونُقِرُّ﴾, and in ﴿ثُمَّ نُخْرِجُكم طِفْلًا﴾. Ibn Abi ʿAbla read these three with yā'. As for the reading with nūn, there are several forms:

First: the famous reading.

Second: al-Sirafi related from Dawud from Yaʿqub: ﴿ونَقُرُّ﴾ with a fatha on the nūn and a ḍamma on the qāf and the rā', from qarra al-māʾ, meaning he poured the water. In another narration from him it is the same, except that the rā' is in the naṣb.

Third: ﴿ونُقِرَّ ونُخْرِجَكم﴾ with a naṣb on the rā' and the jīm.

As for the reading with yā', there are several forms:

First: ﴿يُقَرَّ ويُخْرِجَكم﴾ with a fatha on the qāf, rā', and jīm.

Second: ﴿يُقُرُّ ويُخْرِجُكم﴾ with a ḍamma on the qāf, rā', and jīm.

Third: with a fatha on the yā', a kasra on the qāf, and a ḍamma on the rā'.

Abu Hatim: ﴿ومِنكم مَن يَتَوَفّى﴾ with a fatha on the yā', meaning Allah causes him to die (yatawaffāhu Allāh). Ibn ʿAmra and al-Aʿmash: ﴿العُمْرِ﴾ with the mīm sukūn. The well-known reading is: ﴿ومِنكم مَن يُتَوَفّى ومِنكم مَن يُرَدُّ إلى أرْذَلِ العُمْرِ﴾. In the codex of ʿAbd Allah it is: ﴿ومِنكم مَن يُتَوَفّى ومِنكم مَن يَكُونُ شُيُوخًا﴾, which differs from the well-known reading. Regarding ﴿ورَبَتْ﴾: Abu Jaʿfar read ﴿ورَبَأتْ﴾, meaning it rose high. Al-ʿUmari related from him with softening of the hamza. It was also read ﴿وأنَّهُ باعِثُ﴾.

[Page 8]

**The meanings (al-maʿani):** Know that when He, glorified is He, related their disputation without knowledge concerning the establishment of the gathering and the scattering, and blamed them for it, He presented the proof for the soundness of that in two ways:

One of them: the argument from the creation of the living being first. This agrees with what He summarized in His saying: ﴿Say: He will give them life who brought them into being the first time﴾ [Yasin: 79], and His saying: ﴿They will say: Who will restore us? Say: He who originated you the first time﴾ [al-Isra': 51]. So it is as if He, exalted is He, said: If you are in doubt about what We have promised you of the Resurrection, then reflect on your first creation so that you may know that the One Who is capable of creating you first is capable of creating you again. Then He, glorified is He, mentioned seven stages of the first creation:

The first stage: His saying: ﴿So indeed We created you from dust﴾. In it there are two aspects:

One of them: We created your origin, who is Adam, peace be upon him, from dust, according to His saying: ﴿Like the likeness of Adam; He created him from dust﴾ [Al ʿImran: 59] and His saying: ﴿From it We created you﴾ [Ta-Ha: 55].

The second: that the creation of the human being is from semen and menstrual blood, and these two are only generated from food, and food is either animal or plant. The food of an animal certainly ends, to prevent an infinite regress, at plants, and plants are only generated from earth and water. So His saying ﴿So indeed We created you from dust﴾ is sound.

The second stage: His saying: ﴿Then from a drop﴾. The nutfah is the name for a small amount of water, whatever water it may be, and here it is the water of the male. So it is as if He, glorified is He, says: It is I who transformed that dry dust into delicate water, although there is absolutely no resemblance between the two.

The third stage: His saying: ﴿Then from a clinging clot﴾. The ʿalaqah is a solid piece of blood, and there is no doubt that between water and congealed blood there is a great difference.

The fourth stage: His saying: ﴿Then from a lump of flesh, formed and unformed, that We may make clear to you and settle in the wombs what We will﴾. The mudghah is a small piece of flesh, about the amount that can be chewed. The mukhallaqah is that which is shaped, smooth, and free from defect and flaw. It is said: khallaqa the siwak or the stick, meaning he shaped it and smoothed it, from their saying: a rock that is khalqāʾ, meaning smooth. Then the exegetes have several opinions about it:

One of them: the intended meaning is that in which the states of creation are completed and that in which they are not completed. It is as if He, glorified is He, divided the lump into two parts:

One of them: complete in form, senses, and features; and the second: deficient in these matters. So He made clear that after He made it a lump, some of it He created as a complete human being without deficiency, and some of it not so. This is the saying of Qatada and al-Dahhak. So Allah, exalted is He, creates the lumps varied: some of them are perfect in creation, smooth from defects, and some are the opposite. Following this variation is the variation among people in their creation, forms, height and shortness, completeness and deficiency.

The second: the mukhallaqah is the child who comes out alive, and the ghayr mukhallaqah is the miscarriage. This is the saying of Mujahid.

The third: the mukhallaqah is the shaped and formed, and the ghayr mukhallaqah means the unshaped, which remains as flesh without outline or form. They argued with what ʿAlqamah related from ʿAbd Allah, who said: "When the drop falls into the womb, Allah sends an angel and says: O Lord, is it shaped or unshaped? If He says: unshaped, the wombs expel it as blood. If He says: shaped, he says: O Lord, what is its description? Male or female? What is its provision? What is its term? Is it wretched or happy? Then Allah, glorified is He, says: Go to the Mother of the Book and copy from it the description of this drop. The angel goes and copies it, and remains with it until he reaches the last of its description."

The fourth: al-Qaffal said: al-Takhlīq is derived from al-khalq. Whatever the stages follow upon and whatever creation succeeds creation upon it is the mukhallaq, because of the succession of creation upon it. They said: what is completed is the mukhallaq, and what is not completed is the ghayr mukhallaq, because the successive shapings have not come upon it.

The first opinion is closer, because He, exalted is He, said at the beginning of the verse: ﴿So indeed We created you﴾ and He pointed to mankind, so mukhallaqah and ghayr mukhallaqah must be taken to refer to what will become a human being. That is far-fetched for the miscarriage, because it may be a miscarriage in which the creation was not completed. If it is said: why not take it to refer to the miscarriage because of His saying ﴿and settle in the wombs what We will﴾, which is like an indication that there is in it what He does not settle in the womb, namely the miscarriage? We say: that does not prevent the soundness of what we have mentioned

[Page 9]

concerning the lump being shaped and unshaped, because after He has completed the creation of one part and deficient the creation of another part, it is not necessary that this be completed. Rather, in it there is what Allah settles in the womb and in it there is what He does not settle. Even if He has manifested in it the human form, the miscarriage has entered in this respect.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that We may make clear to you﴾, in it there are two aspects:

One of them: that We may make clear to you that the change of the lump into the shaped is by the choice of the choosing Agent, and were it not for Him, part of it would not have become shaped and part of it unshaped.

The second: the implied meaning is: If you are in doubt about the Resurrection, then indeed We have informed you that We created you from such and such, so that We make clear to you what removes that doubt concerning the matter of your resurrection. For how could the One who is capable of these things be incapable of the return?

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and settle in the wombs what We will for an appointed term﴾, what is meant is the one whom Allah, exalted is He, brings to the limit of birth. The appointed term is the time set for birth, which is the end of six months, or nine, or four years, or whatever Allah, exalted is He, wills and decrees. If He decrees that, it becomes a specified term. The fifth stage: His saying: ﴿Then We bring you out as an infant﴾. He only said "infant" in the singular because the purpose is to indicate the species, and it is possible that each one of you comes out as an infant, as in His saying: ﴿and the angels after that are a supporter﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4]. The sixth stage: His saying: ﴿Then that you may reach your full strength﴾. The ashudd is the perfection of strength, intellect, and discernment, and it is among the plural forms for which no singular has been used. It is as if it is a strength in more than one thing, so it was formed on the plural pattern for that reason. The intended meaning, and Allah knows best, is: then He facilitated for you, in your rearing and your nourishment, matters so that you reach your full strength. Thus He pointed to the states that lie between the emergence of the infant from its mother's belly and the attainment of full strength, and there are intermediate states between them. Some have mentioned that there is no intermediate stage between the state of childhood and the beginning of the state of attaining full strength, to the point that he may reach old age while remaining a child, just as he may be a youth and then enter full strength.

The seventh stage: His saying: ﴿And among you is he who is taken in death, and among you is he who is returned to the most abject age, so that he knows nothing after having known﴾. The meaning is that among you is he who dies in his strength and perfection, and among you is he who is returned to the most abject age, which is decrepitude and senility, so that he becomes as he was at the beginning of his childhood, weak in constitution, feeble in intellect, and little in understanding. If it is said: how does He say ﴿so that he knows nothing after having known﴾ when he knows some things, like the child? We say: the meaning is that his intellect departs so that it is as if he knows nothing, because such a thing may be mentioned in negation for the sake of emphasis. Some people said: this state does not befall believers, because of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then We return him to the lowest of the low, except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Tin: 5–6]. This is weak, because the meaning of His saying ﴿Then We return him to the lowest of the low﴾ is an indication of blame, so what is meant by it is what runs in the manner of punishment, and for that reason He said: ﴿except those who believe and do righteous deeds, for them is a reward never cut off﴾ [al-Tin: 6].

This is the complete argument from the state of the creation of the living being for the soundness of the Resurrection.

The second aspect: the argument from the state of the creation of plants for that. It is His saying, glorified is He and exalted is He: ﴿And you see the earth lifeless﴾. Its hudūd is its drying and its emptiness of plants and greenery. ﴿So when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells﴾. The ihtizaz is movement out of joy, so one hardly says "so-and-so trembled" for such and such unless the matter is of goodness and benefit. So His saying ﴿it stirs and swells﴾ means it moves with plants and expands.

As for His saying: ﴿and it sprouts every lovely kind﴾, it is a metaphor, because from the earth plants grow, while Allah, exalted is He, is the One who causes that to grow; but it is attributed to the earth by way of extension. The meaning of ﴿every lovely kind﴾ is every type of plant, of grain and of trees. Al-bahjah is the beauty and freshness of a thing, and al-bahij has the meaning of the one who delights. Al-Mubarrad said: it is the bright, beautiful thing.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 22, verses 6–7:

ثُمَّ إنَّهُ

(p. 10)

When He, glory be to Him, had established these two proofs, He arranged upon them what is the objective and the conclusion, and He mentioned five matters:

The first: His saying, ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth﴾. The *ḥaqq* (the truth) is that which exists and is established. It is as if He, glory be to Him, made clear that these aspects are indicators of the existence of the Maker (*ṣāniʿ*). Their outcome returns to this: the occurrence of these mutually contrary conditions and their succession upon bodies indicates the existence of the Maker.

The second: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿and that He gives life to the dead﴾. This is an alert that, since it is not deemed far-fetched from God to create these things, how can it be deemed far-fetched from Him to restore the dead?

The third: His saying, ﴿and that He is over all things Powerful﴾. It means that the One from whom the creation of these things is possible must necessarily be, by His essence, one whose power is absolute, and whoever is so is able to do all possible things. Whoever is so must necessarily be able to restore (creation).

The fourth: His saying, ﴿and that the Hour is coming, there is no doubt in it, and that Allah will raise those in the graves﴾. The meaning is that, since He has established the proofs that restoration is possible in itself, and that He, glory be to Him and exalted, is capable of all possible things, it becomes necessary to affirm with certainty that He is capable of restoration in itself. When the possibility is established, and the Truthful One (*al-ṣādiq*) has informed of its occurrence, it is necessary to affirm with certainty that it will occur. Know that the rigorous statement of this proof in the speculative form is to say: restoration is possible in itself, and the Truthful One has informed of its occurrence, so it is necessary to affirm its occurrence with certainty.

As for demonstrating possibility: the proof for it is that these bodies, after their dispersal, are receptive to those attributes that subsisted in them while they were living and rational. The Originator (*al-bāriʾ*), glory be to Him, knows all knowables and is capable of all possible objects of power. This requires affirming with certainty the possibility of restoration, for as we have said, those bodies after their dispersal are receptive to those attributes. For if they were not receptive to them at one time, they would not be receptive to them at any time, because essential matters do not cease. And if they were not receptive to them at any time, they would never have been living and rational at any time. But they were living and rational, so it must be that they are perpetually receptive to these attributes.

As for the claim that the Originator, glory be to Him, is able to bring about that possible thing: it is because He, glory be to Him, knows all knowables, and so He knows the parts of each one of the responsible persons (*mukallafīn*) individually, and He is capable of all possible things, so He is capable of bringing those attributes into those essences. Thus it is established that restoration is possible in itself, and that He, glory be to Him, is able to bring about that possible thing. Therefore it is established that restoration is possible in itself. So when the Truthful One informs of its occurrence, it is necessary to affirm its occurrence with certainty. This is the discourse on establishing this principle.

If it is said: what is the benefit of mentioning the stages of the creation of animals and the creation of plants in this proof? We say: they indicate that He, glory be to Him, is capable of all possible things and knows all knowables. And when that is established, it is established that restoration is possible. For the opponent does not deny the return except on the basis of denying one of these two principles. Accordingly, when Allah, exalted, established the proof for resurrection in His Book, He mentioned together with it His being Powerful and Knowing, as in His saying: ﴿Say: He will give them life who produced them the first time, and He is Knowing of every creation﴾ [Yasin: 79]. So His saying ﴿Say: He will give them life who produced them﴾ is an explanation of power, and His saying ﴿and He is Knowing of every creation﴾ is an explanation of knowledge. And Allah knows best.

Recitation: "ثانِيَ عِطْفِهِ" (thāniya ʿiṭfihi) is read with a kasra on the ʿayn, while al-Hasan alone reads it with a fatha on the ʿayn. * * *

There are issues concerning this verse:

First issue: The scholars differed over who is meant by His saying: ﴿And among people is one who disputes about Allah without knowledge and follows every rebellious devil﴾ [al-Hajj: 3]. There are several views:

The first: Abu Muslim said: The first verse, namely His saying ﴿And among people is one who disputes about Allah without knowledge and follows every rebellious devil﴾, refers to the followers who imitate, and this verse refers to the leaders who are imitated. Both disputants argued without knowledge, even though one of them was a follower and the other a leader. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 22, verses 11–12:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And among people is he who worships Allah on an edge. If good befalls him, he is content with it; but if a trial befalls him, he turns back on his face. He has lost this world and the Hereafter. That is the manifest loss.﴾ ﴿He calls upon, besides Allah, that which neither harms him nor benefits him. That is the far-reaching error.﴾ ﴿He calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit. Wretched is the protector, and wretched is the companion.﴾

The recitation (al-qira'ah, the variant readings): It is read "khasiru al-dunya wal-akhirah" (خاسِرُ الدُّنْيا والآخِرَةِ) with the accusative (naṣb) and with the nominative (raf'). The accusative is as a circumstantial state (ḥal), and the nominative is as the predicate of an omitted subject. In the codex of Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) it reads "man ḍarruhu" (مَن ضَرُّهُ) without the lam.

Know that when He, Exalted is He, explained the state of those who openly associate partners with Allah and dispute concerning it, as we have mentioned, He followed it by mentioning the hypocrites, saying: ﴿And among people is he who worships Allah on an edge (ḥarf).﴾ Regarding the interpretation of "ḥarf" there are two views:

The first: what al-Hasan said, namely that in matters of religion a person relies on the heart and the tongue, and these are the two edges (ḥarfān) of religion. When one of them agrees with the other, he has become complete in religion. But if he displays religion with his tongue for some purposes while hypocrisy is in his heart, it is permissible to say of him, in a tone of blame: he worships Allah on an edge.

The second: His saying "on an edge" (ʿalā ḥarf) means on the fringe of religion, not in its center and heart. This is an illustration of their being in unrest and turmoil in their religion, not in the calm of tranquility, like one who stands on the edge of an army: if he senses booty he settles and is at ease, and otherwise he flees and flies off on his face. This is what is meant by: ﴿If good befalls him, he is content with it; but if a trial befalls him, he turns back on his face.﴾ For steadfastness in religion occurs only if its purpose is attaining the truth, obeying Allah, and fearing His punishment. But if his purpose is immediate good, he displays religion in times of ease and turns away from it in times of hardship, so he is none but a hypocrite, blameworthy. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿wavering between that (MUDHABDHABINA BAYNA DHALIKA)﴾ [al-Nisa': 143], and like His saying: ﴿If there comes to you a victory from Allah, they say, "Were we not with you?"﴾ [al-Nisa': 141].

[Page 13]

The second issue: al-Kalbi said: This verse was revealed concerning Bedouin Arabs who used to come to the Prophet ﷺ in Medina as emigrants from their desert. When one of them was healthy in body, and his mare foaled a fine colt, and his wife bore a boy, and his wealth and livestock increased, he was pleased with it and at ease in it. But if illness befell him, his wife bore a girl, or his mare miscarried, his wealth was lost, and the charity was delayed from him, Satan came to him and said: "These evils have come to you only because of this religion," and so he turned back from his religion. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, Mujahid and Qatadah.

Second: this is the view of al-Dahhak, that it was revealed concerning those whose hearts were to be reconciled (al-mu'allafah qulubuhum), among them Uyaynah ibn Badr, al-Aqra' ibn Habis and al-ʿAbbas ibn Mirdas. Some of them said to others: "Let us enter the religion of Muhammad. If we obtain good, we will know that it is true, and if we obtain other than that, we will know that it is false."

Third: Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: "A man from the Jews embraced Islam, then his sight, his wealth and his child were lost. He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, relieve me (aqilni), for I have obtained no good from this religion of mine: my sight, my child and my wealth have gone.' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Indeed Islam is not said [merely in words]; indeed Islam purifies (yasbiku) as fire purifies the dross of iron, gold and silver.'" Then this verse was revealed.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿and if a trial befalls him, he turns back on his face﴾, there are questions concerning it:

The first: How does He say "and if a trial befalls him, he turns back on his face," when good is also a trial, since it is a test? He, Exalted is He, says: ﴿And We test you with evil and good as a trial﴾. The answer: Such usage is common in the language, for blessing is also a trial and a test, as in His saying: ﴿As for man, when his Lord tests him and honors him and blesses him﴾ [al-Fajr: 15]. But the term "trial" (balaʾ) is applied only to what is heavy upon the natural disposition. The hypocrite has no good except worldly good, and has no evil except worldly evil, because he has no religion. Therefore the verse came according to what they believe, even though all good is a trial; but the term is used most frequently for what is severe and weighs heavily.

The second question: If the verse concerns the hypocrite, what is the meaning of His saying "turns back on his face," when in reality he never became a Muslim so as to turn back and apostatize? The answer: What is meant is that he displayed with his tongue the opposite of what he had displayed before. He began to disparage religion in times of hardship, whereas previously he had praised it, and this is a turning in reality.

The third question: Muqatil said: "Good" is the opposite of "evil," so when He said "if good befalls him, he is content with it," it should have been said: "and if evil befalls him, he turns back on his face." The answer: Since hardship is not in itself ugly, He, Exalted is He, did not say "and if evil befalls him," but described it with what does not indicate ugliness.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He has lost this world and the Hereafter﴾, that is because in this world he loses honor, dignity, attaining booty, eligibility for martyrdom, leadership and judgeship, and his property and blood are not kept safe. As for the Hereafter, he forfeits lasting reward and incurs lasting punishment: ﴿That is the manifest loss.﴾

As for His saying: ﴿He calls upon, besides Allah, that which neither harms him nor benefits him﴾, the closer view is that it refers to the polytheist who worships idols. This is like an indication that the verse was not revealed concerning the Jew, because he is not among those who call upon idols besides Allah. The closer view is that it was revealed concerning the polytheists who attached themselves to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in a manner of hypocrisy. He, Exalted is He, explained that: ﴿That is the far-reaching error,﴾ and meant by it the greatness of their error and disbelief. It is also possible that He meant by it how far their error was from the truth, because all of it, although it shares in being mistaken, some of it is farther from the truth than others. The "far-reaching error" is borrowed from the error of one who is driven far into the wilderness as a wanderer, and whose distance of error has grown long and far.

The answer: Such usage is common in the language, for blessing is also a trial and a test, as in His saying: ﴿As for man, when his Lord tests him and honors him and blesses him﴾ [al-Fajr: 15]. But the term "trial" (balaʾ) is applied only to what is heavy upon the natural disposition. The hypocrite has no good except worldly good, and has no evil except worldly evil, because he has no religion. Therefore the verse came according to what they believe, even though all good is a trial; but the term is used most frequently for what is severe and weighs heavily.

The second question: If the verse concerns the hypocrite, what is the meaning of His saying "turns back on his face," when in reality he never became a Muslim so as to turn back and apostatize? The answer: What is meant is that he displayed with his tongue the opposite of what he had displayed before. He began to disparage religion in times of hardship, whereas previously he had praised it, and this is a turning in reality.

The third question: Muqatil said: "Good" is the opposite of "evil," so when He said "if good befalls him, he is content with it," it should have been said: "and if evil befalls him, he turns back on his face." The answer: Since hardship is not in itself ugly, He, Exalted is He, did not say "and if evil befalls him," but described it with what does not indicate ugliness.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He has lost this world and the Hereafter﴾, that is because in this world he loses honor, dignity, attaining booty, eligibility for martyrdom, leadership and judgeship, and his property and blood are not kept safe. As for the Hereafter, he forfeits lasting reward and incurs lasting punishment: ﴿That is the manifest loss.﴾

As for His saying: ﴿He calls upon, besides Allah, that which neither harms him nor benefits him﴾, the closer view is that it refers to the polytheist who worships idols. This is like an indication that the verse was not revealed concerning the Jew, because he is not among those who call upon idols besides Allah. The closer view is that it was revealed concerning the polytheists who attached themselves to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in a manner of hypocrisy. He, Exalted is He, explained that: ﴿That is the far-reaching error,﴾ and meant by it the greatness of their error and disbelief. It is also possible that He meant by it how far their error was from the truth, because all of it, although it shares in being mistaken, some of it is farther from the truth than others. The "far-reaching error" is borrowed from the error of one who is driven far into the wilderness as a wanderer, and whose distance of error has grown long and far.

**Question One:** Regarding His saying, ﴿He calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit﴾, there are two issues.

**Issue One:** The scholars differed in its interpretation in two ways.

The first is that what is meant is their leaders, whom they used to turn to for help, because it is possible for them to cause harm. The proof for this view is that God, exalted is He, stated in the previous verse that the idols neither harm them nor benefit them. This verse requires that the one mentioned in it be harmful and beneficial. So if the one mentioned in this verse were the idols, there would be a contradiction.

The second view is that what is meant is the idol. The proponents of this view answered the charge of contradiction in several ways:

First, the idols do not harm or benefit by themselves, but worshipping them is the cause of harm, and this is enough to attribute the harm to them. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿My Lord, indeed they have led many of the people astray﴾ [Ibrahim: 36]. He attributed the leading astray to them in the sense that they were a cause of straying. Similarly here, He negated harm from them in the first verse in the sense of their being agents, and He attributed harm to them in this verse in the sense that worshipping them is the cause of harm.

Second, it is as if He, glorified and exalted is He, stated in the first verse that they in reality neither harm nor benefit, then said in the second verse: Even if we concede that they are harmful and beneficial, their harm is greater than their benefit.

Third, if the disbelievers were fair, they would know that nothing benefit or harm comes from them in this world. Then, in the Hereafter, they will witness the great punishment caused by worshipping them. So it is as if they are saying to them in the Hereafter: Your harm is greater than your benefit.

**Issue Two:** The grammarians differed regarding the i'rab (the grammatical analysis of the case endings) of His saying: ﴿for one whose harm is nearer﴾ [لَمَن ضَرُّهُ أقْرَبُ].

As for His saying: ﴿Wretched is the patron, and wretched is the companion﴾ [لَبِئْسَ المَوْلى ولَبِئْسَ العَشِيرُ]: *al-mawlā* is the protector and helper, and *al-ʿashīr* is the companion and associate. Know that this description fits the leaders better, because *al-mawlā* is hardly used for idols. Thus God, exalted is He, stated that they turn away from the worship of God, who combines the good of this world and the Hereafter, to the worship of idols and to obedience to the leaders. Then He blamed the leaders with His saying: ﴿Wretched is the patron﴾, and what is meant is the blame of whoever seeks support from them and takes refuge with them.

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ يُدْخِلُ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وعَمِلُوا الصّالِحاتِ جَنّاتٍ تَجْرِي مِن تَحْتِها الأنْهارُ إنَّ اللَّهَ يَفْعَلُ ما يُرِيدُ﴾ ﴿مَن كانَ يَظُنُّ أنْ لَنْ يَنْصُرَهُ اللَّهُ في الدُّنْيا والآخِرَةِ فَلْيَمْدُدْ بِسَبَبٍ إلى السَّماءِ ثُمَّ لِيَقْطَعْ فَلْيَنْظُرْ هَلْ يُذْهِبَنَّ كَيْدُهُ ما يَغِيظُ﴾ ﴿وكَذَلِكَ أنْزَلْناهُ آياتٍ بَيِّناتٍ وأنَّ اللَّهَ يَهْدِي مَن يُرِيدُ﴾

Know that when He, glory be to Him, had explained in the previous verse the state of the worship of the hypocrites and the state of their object of worship, in this verse He explained the nature of the worship of the believers and the nature of their object of worship. As for their worship, it was upon a path whose correctness is impossible, and as for their object of worship, [it] "neither harms nor benefits." As for the believers, their worship is genuine, and their object of worship gives them the greatest benefits, which is Paradise. Then He explained the perfection of Paradise, which combines crops and trees, and that rivers flow beneath it. And He, exalted is He, explained that He does what He wills for them of various kinds of bounty and kindness, in addition to their rewards, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So He will give them their full rewards and increase them from His bounty﴾ [al-Nisa: 173].

Our companions argued concerning the creation of acts with His words, glory be to Him: ﴿Indeed, Allah does what He wills﴾. They said: We are agreed that He, glory be to Him, wills faith, and the word "ma" (what) is general, so it is necessary that He be the doer of faith, by His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does what He wills﴾. Al-Ka'bi answered this by saying that Allah, exalted is He, does what He wills to do, not what He wills for someone else to do. The reply: His saying "what He wills" is more general than our saying "what He wills to do," and more general than our saying "what He wills for someone else to do," so restricting it is contrary to the text.

Regarding His saying, ﴿Whoever thinks that Allah will not help him in this world and the Hereafter﴾, to what does the pronoun "him" refer? There are two opinions.

The first, which is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Kalbi, Muqatil, al-Dahhak, Qatadah, Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi, and which al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj preferred, is that it refers to Muhammad (ﷺ). The meaning is: whoever thinks that Allah will not help Muhammad (ﷺ) in this world, by raising His word and making His religion prevail, and in the Hereafter, by raising his rank and avenging himself on those who denied him. Although the Messenger (ﷺ) has not been mentioned in the verse, there is something in it that indicates him, namely the mention of faith in His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah will admit those who believe﴾, and faith is not complete except through Allah and His Messenger. Therefore, two matters must be investigated here:

The first: Who were the ones who thought that Allah, exalted is He, would not help Muhammad (ﷺ)?

The second: What is the meaning of His saying, ﴿Then let him extend a rope to the sky and then cut it off﴾?

As for the first investigation, they mentioned several views:

One of them: Some of the Muslims, out of intense rage and fury at the polytheists, were impatient for the victory that Allah had promised His Messenger, so this verse was revealed.

The second: Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning a group from Asad and Ghatafan who said: "We fear that Allah will not help Muhammad, so the agreement between us and our allies among the Jews will be cut off, and they will not supply us with food."

The third: His envious ones and enemies were expecting that Allah would not help him or make him triumph over his enemies, so whenever they witnessed that Allah had helped him, it enraged them.

As for the second investigation: Know that regarding the word "sabab" (cause, means, rope) there are two views. The first is that it means a rope. Those who held this view differed concerning "the sky." Some said it is the roof of the house, and some said it is the sky in its literal sense. They said: The meaning is: whoever thinks that Allah will not help him, and then is enraged that he does not attain what he seeks, let him exhaust his capacity to remove what enrages him, by doing what one does when rage reaches its utmost limit, until he extends a rope to the roof of his house and hangs himself, so let him see whether, by doing that, the help of Allah which enrages him will disappear. According to this view, they differed concerning "cutting" (qat'). Some said: He called the hanging "cutting," because the one who hangs himself cuts off his breath by blocking its passages. He called his action "scheming" (kayd) because he placed it where scheming would be, since he could not do otherwise, or by way of mockery; however, he did not scheme against the one he envies, but rather against himself. The meaning is: he has nothing in his hand except what does not remove what enrages him. This is the view of al-Kalbi and Muqatil. Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said: He ties the rope to his neck and to the ceiling of the house, then cuts the rope until he chokes and dies. All of this applies if we understand "the sky" as the roof of the house, and this is the view of many exegetes.

Others said: What is meant is the sky itself, for it is possible to understand the statement as referring to the sky itself, and this is preferable to understanding it as the roof of the house, because the latter is only understood with a qualification. Moreover, the purpose is not a command to do that; rather, the purpose is that this should turn him away from his rage toward obedience to Allah, exalted is He. When this is so, the more remote the mentioned act is from possibility, the more fitting it is that it be the intended meaning. It is known that extending a rope to the sky of this world and hanging oneself with it is more remote in possibility than extending it to the roof of the house, because the latter is possible.

As for those who said that the "sabab" is not the rope, they mentioned two views:

The first: It is as if He said: "Let him extend a means to the sky, then let him cut, by that means, the distance, then let him see, for he will know that, despite enduring hardship in what he thought, he has suffered a losing bargain, as if he had done nothing." This is the view of Abu Muslim.

The second: It is as if He said: "Let him seek a means by which he may reach the sky, and then let him cut off Allah's help to His Prophet, and let him see whether it is possible for him to reach the sky by some stratagem, and whether it is possible for him to cut off by that Allah's help from His Messenger. If that is impossible, then his rage is of no benefit." Know that the purpose in all these views is clear, for it is a rebuke to the disbelievers for raging over what is of no benefit, and it has the same meaning as His saying: ﴿So if you are able to seek a tunnel into the earth or a ladder into the sky﴾ [al-An'am: 35], thereby making clear that he has no way to bring about the signs they demanded.

The second opinion: The pronoun in His saying, ﴿Allah will not help him﴾, refers to the one mentioned at the beginning of the verse, because he is the one mentioned, and it is required that a pronoun refer to a previously mentioned antecedent when that is possible. Those who held this view understood "help" as "provision." Abu ʿUbaydah said: A beggar from Banu Bakr stopped before us and said: "Whoever helps me, may Allah help him," meaning: whoever gives me, may Allah give him. So it is as if He said: "Whoever thinks that Allah will not provide for him in this world and the Hereafter, then because of this thought he turns away from adhering to the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ), as He described him in His saying: ﴿And if a trial afflicts him, he turns back on his face﴾ [al-Hajj: 11], and he reaches the utmost degree of despair, which is choking, for that does not overcome the naming, and it makes him one who is provided for."

As for His saying, ﴿And thus We have sent it down as clear verses﴾, its meaning is: In the same manner of this sending down, We have sent down the entire Qur'an as clear verses.

As for His saying, ﴿And that Allah guides whom He wills﴾, our companions have argued by it, saying: The guidance meant is either the placing of proofs or the creation of knowledge. The first is not permissible, because He has done that for all the accountable, and because His saying, "guides whom He wills," is evidence that guidance is not obligatory upon Him, but is contingent upon His will, glory be to Him, whereas placing proofs before the opponent is obligatory. So what remains is that what is meant is the creation of knowledge. Qadi ʿAbd al-Jabbar said in al-Itimad: This admits of several meanings:

One of them: He imposes obligations upon whom He wills, because whoever imposes something upon someone has described it to him and made it clear to him.

The second: What is meant is that He guides to Paradise and reward whomever He wills among those who believe and do righteous deeds.

The third: What is meant is that Allah, exalted is He, shows kindness to whomever He wills, of those whom He knows that, if He increases them in guidance, they will remain steadfast in their faith, as in His saying, ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance﴾. This is the view that al-Hasan alluded to when he said: "Allah guides whoever accepts, not whoever does not accept." The first two views were mentioned by Abu ʿAli. As for the answer to the first: Allah, exalted is He, mentioned this after the explanation of the proofs and the answer to doubts, so it is not permissible to restrict it to mere imposition of obligation. As for the last two, they are rejected, because according to you they are obligatory upon Allah, exalted is He, whereas His saying, "whom He wills," implies that they are not obligatory.
