Page 17

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Sabians, and the Christians, and the Magians, and those who associate others with Allah — indeed, Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, Allah is over all things Witness.﴾ ﴿Have you not seen that to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, and the sun and the moon and the stars and the mountains and the trees and the moving creatures, and many of mankind? But many have deserved the punishment. And whoever Allah humiliates, there is none to honor him. Indeed, Allah does what He wills.﴾

The recitation: It was read as "ḥuqqa" (حُقَّ) with a damma, and it was read as "ḥaqqan" (حَقًّا), meaning "the punishment has been decreed upon him, as a decree." It was also read "mukramin" (مُكْرَمٍ) with a fatha on the ra', meaning "honoring" (the act of honoring). Know that when He, Exalted is He, said ﴿And that Allah guides whom He wills﴾, He followed it in this verse by explaining who He guides and who He does not guide.

Know that a Muslim's differences in the fundamental matters (al-masa'il al-usuliyya, the foundational doctrinal questions) are only with three categories:

The first: those who share with him the prophethood of his Prophet, such as the disagreement between the Jabriyya (determinists, who deny human agency in actions) and the Qadariyya (proponents of human free will) over the creation of human actions, and the disagreement between those who affirm the divine attributes and the vision of God and those who deny them.

The second: those who differ with him about prophethood but share with him the acknowledgment of the Chooser, the free agent, such as the disagreement between the Muslims, the Jews and the Christians about the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), Jesus and Moses, peace be upon them both.

The third: those who differ with him about God. These are the Sophists (al-Sufasta'iyya), who suspend judgment about realities; the Dahriyya (naturalists), who do not acknowledge the existence of any agent affecting the world; and the philosophers (al-Falasifa), who affirm an agent that acts by necessity rather than by choice.

If the differences occurring in the foundations of religions are confined to these three categories, then there is no doubt that the greatest aspect of disagreement comes from the last category. This last category, with its three divisions, is not found in the world among those who openly display their beliefs and doctrines; rather, they remain hidden.

As for the second category, the disagreement arising because of the prophets, peace be upon them, its division is as follows: It is said that those who affirm the free agent either acknowledge the existence of prophets or do not. If they acknowledge it, they are either followers of one who was truly a prophet, or of one who was a pretender to prophethood. The followers of the prophets, peace be upon them, are the Muslims, the Jews and the Christians, and another sect between the Jews and the Christians, who are the Sabians. The followers of the pretender are the Magians. As for those who deny the prophets absolutely, they are the worshippers of idols and images, and they are called the polytheists (al-mushrikun), and the Barahima (Brahmins) enter among them, according to the differences in their classes.

Thus it is established that the religions arising from the disagreements concerning the prophets, peace be upon them, are these six that Allah, Exalted is He, mentioned in this verse. Qatada and Muqatil said: "The religions are six: one belongs to Allah, Exalted is He, and it is Islam, and five belong to Satan." The full discussion of this verse has already been given in Surat al-Baqara.

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection﴾, there are two issues:

The first issue: Al-Zajjaj said: This is the predicate (khabar) of Allah's saying ﴿Indeed, those who believe﴾, just as you say: "Indeed, your brother, indeed the debt upon him is great." Jarir said:

Indeed, the Caliph, indeed Allah has clothed him
With the garment of kingship, by which the outcomes are hoped for.

The second issue: The word "separation" (al-fasl) is unrestricted, so it may include separating them in all states and places. He does not reward them with one reward without difference, nor does He gather them in one place. It was also said: "He will separate between them" means "He will judge between them."

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things Witness﴾, the meaning is that He separates between them while knowing what each of them deserves, so no injustice or wrongdoing occurs in that separation.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 22, verse 18:

Page 18

As for His saying, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿Have you not seen that to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth﴾, there are questions concerning it.

The first question: What is "seeing" (al-ru'yah) here? The answer: It means knowledge, i.e., "Do you not know that to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth?" He knew this only through the report of Allah, not because he saw it.

The second question: What is prostration (al-sujud) here? We say: there are several views.

The first: Al-Zajjaj said: The best of the views on the prostration of these things is that they prostrate in obedience to Allah, the Exalted. This is like His saying: ﴿Then He turned to the heaven when it was smoke and said to it and to the earth, "Come willingly or unwillingly." They said, "We have come willingly"﴾ [Fussilat: 11]; ﴿that We say to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [An-Nahl: 40]; ﴿And indeed, among them is that which descends out of fear of Allah﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 74]; ﴿And there is not a thing but it exalts [Allah] with His praise﴾ [Al-Isra': 44]; ﴿And We subjected the mountains to exalt [Allah] with David﴾. The meaning is that these bodies, since they are receptive to all the accidents (a'rad) that Allah, the Exalted, produces in them without any refusal whatsoever, resemble obedience and submission, which is prostration. If it is said: this interpretation is refuted by His saying: ﴿and many of mankind﴾, for prostration in the sense I have mentioned is general to all people, so attributing it to "many of them" would be specification without benefit. The answer has several aspects:

First: Although prostration in the sense we have mentioned is general with regard to all, some of them rebelled and became arrogant and abandoned prostration outwardly. This individual, although prostrating by his essence, is rebellious by his outward state, whereas the believer prostrates both by his essence and by his outward state. Because of this difference, specification by mention occurred.

Second: We cut off His saying ﴿and many of mankind﴾ from what precedes it, and in this there are three aspects:

The first: We say: the construction of the verse is: "And to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, and many of mankind prostrate to Him," so the first prostration is in the sense of submission, and the second in the sense of obedience and worship. We did this because evidence has established that it is not permissible to use a homonymous word in all its meanings together.

The second: That His saying ﴿and many of mankind﴾ is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted, and it is paired (muthabb), because the predicate of its counterpart indicates it, namely His saying: ﴿the punishment has become due upon him﴾.

The third: That he exaggerates in multiplying those upon whom punishment is due, so that he conjoins "many" with "many," then gives information about them that "the punishment has become due upon them," as if it were said: "And many of mankind, and many upon whom the punishment has become due."

Third: Whoever permits using a homonymous word in both its senses says: the intended meaning of prostration with respect to rational living beings is worship, and with respect to inanimate things is submission. Whoever denies this says: Allah, the Exalted, spoke with this word twice, so He meant by it obedience with respect to rational beings, and submission with respect to inanimate things.

The third question: His saying: ﴿And to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ [Al-Ra'd: 15] has the wording of generality, so mankind enters into it. Why then did He say again: ﴿and many of mankind﴾? The answer: If He had restricted Himself to what preceded, it would have given the impression that all mankind prostrate just as all the angels prostrate. So He clarified that many of them prostrate willingly, while many of them refrain from that, and they are those upon whom the punishment has become due.

The second view on the interpretation of prostration: Everything other than Allah, the Exalted, is possible in its essence (mumkin li-dhatihi), and that which is possible in its essence does not have its existence preferred over its non-existence except upon reaching the Necessary in its essence (wajib li-dhatihi), as He said: ﴿And that to your Lord is the finality﴾ [An-Najm: 42]. And just as possibility is necessarily attached to the possible at the time of its coming into being and its continuance, so its need of the Necessary exists at the time of its coming into being and at the time of its continuance. This essential need, which is necessarily attached to the quiddity, is more indicative of humility and lowliness than placing the forehead upon the ground, for that is a conventional sign of essential need, which may admit of truth and falsehood. As for essential need itself, it is impossible for it to change or be altered. Therefore all possible things prostrate in this sense to Allah, the Exalted, that is, they are humbled, abased, acknowledging their poverty toward Him and their need for His creation and bringing-into-being. On this basis they interpreted His saying: ﴿And there is not a thing but it exalts [Allah] with His praise﴾ [Al-Isra': 44].

Page 19

This is the view of al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him. The third view: that the prostration of these things is the prostration of their shadows, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whose shadows incline from the right and the left, prostrating to Allah while they are humbled﴾ [An-Nahl: 48]. This is the view of Mujahid.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿and many of mankind, and many upon whom the punishment has become due﴾, Ibn 'Abbas, in the narration of 'Ata', said: "And many of mankind" means those who affirm His oneness, and "many upon whom the punishment has become due" means those who do not affirm His oneness. It is also narrated from him that he said: "And many of mankind" means those in Paradise. This narration confirms what we mentioned, that His saying ﴿and many of mankind﴾ is a subject whose predicate is omitted. Others said: pause at His saying ﴿and many of mankind﴾, then begin anew, saying: ﴿and many, the punishment has become due upon them﴾, i.e., it became obligatory because of their refusal and their abstention from prostration.

* * *

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever Allah humiliates, for him there is no honorer﴾, the meaning is that for those upon whom the punishment has become due there is no one who is able to remove that humiliation from them so that he would be an honorer of them. Then He explained by His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does what He wills﴾ that it is He alone from whom honor and humiliation on the Day of Resurrection, through reward and punishment, are rightly issued. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 22, verses 19–24:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord. As for those who disbelieve, garments of fire will be cut out for them, and boiling water will be poured over their heads﴾ ﴿by which whatever is in their bellies and their skins will be melted﴾ ﴿And for them are maces of iron﴾ ﴿Every time they wish to get out of it from distress, they will be returned into it, and [it will be said], "Taste the punishment of the burning."﴾ ﴿Indeed, Allah will admit those who believed and did righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow. They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their clothing therein will be silk﴾ ﴿And they were guided to good speech and were guided to the path of the Praiseworthy﴾.

The recitation: It is narrated from al-Kisa'i that "khisman" (adversaries) is read with a kasra on the kha'. It is also read "qutti'at" with the lightening (takhfif) [i.e., qutti'at without the doubling of the ta']; as if God decrees for them fires according to the measures of their bodies, enveloping them, just as worn garments are cut. Al-A'mash read: "Every time they wish to get out of it from distress, they are returned into it." Al-Hasan read "yusahharu" with a doubled ha' for emphasis. It is also read "wa lu'lu'an" in the accusative, on the assumption of "wa yu'tawna lu'lu'an" (and they will be given pearls), like His saying "wa huran 'inan" (and wide-eyed maidens). And "lu'lu'an" with the second hamza changed to a waw.

Know that when He, glory be to Him, made clear that people are of two kinds, some who prostrate to Allah and some upon whom the punishment is justly due, He mentioned here the manner of their disputing. There are several issues in this:

First issue: Those who hold that the minimum of plurality is two argue from His saying, "These two adversaries dispute." The answer: "khasm" (adversary) is an adjective describing a group or a party, so it is as if it were said: "These are two groups or parties that dispute." Thus His saying "hadhani" (these two) is in accordance with the wording, and "ikhtasamu" (they disputed) is in accordance with the meaning, like His saying: "And among them are those who listen to you, until when they go out..." [Muhammad: 16].

Second issue: They have mentioned several interpretations of "the two adversaries":

The first: What is meant is the group of believers and their community, and the group of disbelievers and their community, and that all disbelievers are included in this. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it refers to the people of the six religions. "Concerning their Lord" means concerning His essence and His attributes.

The second: It is narrated that the People of the Book said: "We have more right to Allah than you, and our book is older than yours, and our prophet came before your prophet." And the believers said: "We have more right to Allah; we believed in Muhammad and in your prophet and in what Allah sent down of Scripture, while you know our book and our prophet, then you abandoned them and disbelieved in them out of envy." This is their dispute concerning their Lord.

The third: Qays ibn 'Ubada narrated from Abu Dharr al-Ghifari, may Allah have mercy on him, that he used to swear by Allah that this verse was revealed concerning six men from Quraysh who fought in single combat on the Day of Badr: Hamza, 'Ali, 'Ubayda ibn al-Harith, 'Utba and Shayba, the two sons of Rabi'a, and al-Walid ibn 'Utba. 'Ali, peace be upon him, said: "I am the first to kneel down for the dispute before Allah, exalted is He, on the Day of Resurrection."

The fourth: 'Ikrima said: they are Paradise and Hellfire. Hellfire said: "Allah created me for His punishment." Paradise said: "Allah created me for His mercy." So Allah related their account to Muhammad ﷺ.

The closest view is the first, because although the occasion of revelation is specific, it is obligatory to take the speech according to its apparent meaning. His saying "these" is like a reference to what was previously mentioned, namely the people of the six religions. Also, He mentioned two categories: the people of His obedience and the people of disobedience upon whom the punishment is due, so it must be that the reference of this returns to these two. Whoever restricts it to the polytheists of Arabia or to the Jews, on account of what they said in their book and about their prophet that we have related, has erred. This is what His saying indicates: "Indeed, Allah will judge between them" [al-Hajj: 17], meaning judgment. For mentioning dispute requires that what follows it be a judgment; so Allah, exalted is He, made clear His ruling regarding the disbelievers, and He mentioned three matters of their condition:

The first: His saying, "Garments of fire will be cut out for them." The meaning of "garments" is the fire encompassing them, like His saying: "For them there will be a bed of Hellfire, and above them coverings" [al-A'raf: 41]. This is narrated from Anas. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it is of brass melted by fire, taking it from His saying: "Their garments will be of pitch" [Ibrahim: 50]. The speech is expressed in the past tense, like His saying: "And the Horn is blown" [Ya-Sin: 51] and "And every soul will come with it, a driver and a witness" [Qaf: 21], because what pertains to the Hereafter is as if it has occurred.

The second: His saying, "Boiling water will be poured over their heads. By it whatever is in their bellies and their skins will be melted." "Hamim" is hot water. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: if a single drop of it fell upon the mountains of this world, it would melt them. "Yusharu" means "yudhabu" (is melted). That is, when the boiling water is poured over their heads, its effect inwardly is like its effect outwardly, so it melts their intestines and inner organs just as it melts their skins. This is more emphatic than His saying: "And they are given boiling water, which cuts their intestines to pieces" [Muhammad: 15].

The third: His saying, "And for them are maces of iron." "Maqami'" are whips. And in a hadith: "If one of them were placed upon the earth and all the two weights [humans and jinn] gathered to lift it, they would not be able to lift it."

As for His saying, "Every time they wish to get out of it from distress, they will be returned into it," know that returning does not occur except after exiting. The meaning is: every time they wish to get out of it from distress, and they come out, they are returned into it. The meaning of "coming out" is what is related from al-Hasan, that the fire strikes them with its flames and lifts them up, until when they are at its top, they are struck with maces and they fall into it for seventy autumns. It is said to them: "Taste the punishment of the burning." "Hariq" is the intense fire, the great destroyer.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned His ruling regarding the believers in four aspects:

صفحة ٢١ (page 21)

The first: The dwelling, which is His saying: "Indeed, Allah will admit those who believed and did righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow." The second: The adornment, which is His saying: "They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their clothing therein will be silk." He, exalted is He, made clear that He will bring them in the Hereafter to what He forbade them in this world of these matters, though the one who permitted it for them also shares in it, because what is permitted for women in this world is small in comparison to what will be attained for them in the Hereafter. The third: The garments, which is His saying: "And their clothing therein will be silk." The fourth: His saying: "And they were guided to good speech." Concerning it there are several views:

The first: The testimony that there is no god but Allah is "the good speech," because of His saying: "A good word like a good tree" [Ibrahim: 24] and His saying: "To Him good words ascend" [Fatir: 10]. And "the path of the Praiseworthy" is according to His saying: "And indeed, you guide to a straight path" [al-Shura: 52].

The second: al-Suddi said: "And they were guided to good speech" is the Qur'an.

The third: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, in the narration of 'Ata', said: it is their saying: "Praise be to Allah who has fulfilled His promise to us."

The fourth: When they travel to the Abode of the Hereafter, they are guided to the glad tidings that come to them from Allah, exalted is He, of enduring bliss, joy and peace. This is the meaning of His saying: "And the angels will enter upon them from every gate: 'Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured. How excellent is the final abode'" [al-Ra'd: 23]. And in my view there is a fifth aspect: that the bodily attachment serves as a veil for human souls in their connection to the world of holiness; when they separate from their bodies, the covering is removed and the divine lights shine forth. The manifestation of those lights is what is meant by His saying: "And they were guided to good speech and were guided to the path of the Praiseworthy," and the expression of them is what is meant by His saying: "And they were guided to good speech."

There is a difficulty in this: how did He join the future tense, which is His saying ﴿and bar [others] from the way of Allah﴾, to the past tense, which is His saying ﴿disbelieve﴾? The answer to this is from two aspects.

The first: It is said, "So-and-so is generous to the poor and helps the weak." This does not refer to a present state or a future one; rather it indicates the continuous existence of this generosity from him at all of his times and occasions. It is as if it were said: "Indeed, those who disbelieve have among their characteristics the barring from the way of Allah." A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Those who believe, and whose hearts are assured by the remembrance of Allah﴾ [al-Ra'd: 28].

The second: Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: The estimation is: "Indeed, those who disbelieved in the past, and they now bar [others]," and it includes that they do this in the present and the future. As for His saying ﴿and the Sacred Mosque﴾, it means: and they also bar them from the Sacred Mosque. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: The verse was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan ibn Harb and his companions, when they barred the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah from the Sacred Mosque, from performing Hajj and 'Umrah and slaughtering the offering (hady). So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) disliked fighting them, and he was in the state of ihram for 'Umrah. Then they concluded a treaty with him that he would return in the following year.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿which We have made for the people equal, the resident therein and the visitor﴾, there are issues concerning it:

The first issue: Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: That is, We have made it for the people a place of rites (manasik) and worship. His saying ﴿equal, the resident therein and the visitor﴾ is in the nominative case, as the predicate of a fronted subject; the meaning is: the resident therein and the visitor are equal. The estimation of the verse is: the Sacred Mosque which We have made a place of rites for the people, so the resident therein and the visitor are equal. Asim and Ya'qub read ﴿sawa'an﴾ with the accusative, by making the act of making (ja'l) apply to it, because the verb ja'ala takes two objects. And Allah knows best.

The second issue: The resident (al-'akif) is the one who stays there and is present. The visitor (al-badi) is the one who comes from the desert (badw), and he is the one who yearns towards it from his tribe. Some of them said: Included among the resident is the one who is near, if he settles and remains there for worship, even if he is not from its people.

The third issue: They differed concerning in what respect the two are equal. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said in some narrations: They are equal in dwelling in Makkah and residing in it. So neither of them has more right to the dwelling in which he is than the other, except that one of them has preceded to the dwelling. This is the view of Qatadah and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Among the position of these people is that renting and selling the houses of Makkah is forbidden, and they argued for it with the verse and a report. As for the verse, it is this one. They said: The land of Makkah is not to be owned, for if it were owned, the resident therein and the visitor would not be equal. Since they are equal, it has been established that its status is the status of the mosques. As for the report, it is His saying (peace be upon him): "Makkah is permissible for whoever precedes to it." This is the view of Ibn 'Umar, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, and the view of Abu Hanifah and Ishaq al-Handhali (may Allah be pleased with them). According to this, what is meant by "the Sacred Mosque" is the whole Haram, because using the expression "the Sacred Mosque" to mean the city is permissible, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Isra': 1]. And here the indication is established by His saying ﴿the resident﴾, because what is meant by it is one who stays in residence, and his residence is not in the mosque but in homes. So it must be said: He mentioned the mosque and meant Makkah.

The second view: What is meant is that Allah made the people equal in worship in the mosque: the resident is not entitled to prevent the visitor, and vice versa. He (peace be upon him) said: "O Banu 'Abd Manaf, whoever among you is given charge of any affair of the people, let him not prevent anyone who circumambulates this House or prays at any hour of the night or day." This is the saying of al-Hasan and Mujahid, and the view of those who permitted the selling of the houses of Makkah. A debate took place between al-Shafi'i and Ishaq al-Handhali in Makkah, and Ishaq did not grant a concession in renting the houses of Makkah. Al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him) argued with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who were expelled from their homes without right﴾ [al-Hajj: 40], so the home was attributed to its owner and to one who is not its owner. He (peace be upon him) also said on the day of the Conquest of Makkah: "Whoever closes his door is safe." And he (ﷺ) said: "Did 'Aqil leave us any house?" 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) bought the house of the prison. Do you think he bought it from its owner or from one who was not its owner? Ishaq said: When I knew that the proof had bound me, I abandoned my view.

As for what they said about carrying the word "mosque" to mean Makkah by the indication of His saying "the resident," it is weak, because "the resident" may mean one who is constantly attached to the mosque, the one who performs i'tikaf therein continuously or for most of the time, so what they mentioned does not necessarily follow. It is also possible that "the resident" means the neighbour of the mosque who is firmly established in worship therein at every time. So there is no reason to turn the speech away from its apparent meaning in the face of these possibilities.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿and whoever intends therein deviation with injustice﴾, there are issues concerning it:

[Page 23]

The first issue: It was read "yarid" with a fatha on the yā', from al-wurud (arriving), and its meaning is: whoever comes to it with deviation. It is reported from al-Hasan: "and whoever intends its deviation with injustice." The meaning is: whoever intends to commit deviation therein. The idafah (annexation) is sound through the figurative extension in the adverbial noun (zarf), like "the plotting of the night and the day." Its meaning is: whoever intends to deviate therein as a wrongdoer.

The second issue: Ilhad (deviation) is turning away from the intended course, and its origin is the "ilhad" of the digger (who digs a side-tunnel). The exegetes mentioned several opinions concerning the explanation of ilhad:

One of them: It is shirk. That is, whoever takes refuge in the sanctuary of Allah in order to commit shirk, Allah will punish him. This is one of the reports from Ibn 'Abbas, and the saying of 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatadah and Muqatil.

The second: Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: It was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Sa'd, when the Prophet (ﷺ) pardoned him, and he apostatised and became a polytheist; and concerning Qays ibn Dababah. Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Khatal, when he killed an Ansari and fled to Makkah as a disbeliever, so the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered his killing on the day of the Conquest while he was a disbeliever.

The third: killing game (sayd) that Allah has forbidden.

The fourth: entering Makkah without ihram and committing what is not lawful for the one in ihram.

The fifth: that it is hoarding (ihtikar), from Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The sixth: preventing its construction and maintenance.

The seventh: from 'Ata': a man's saying in a transaction: "No, by Allah," and "Yes, by Allah." And from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar that he had two tents, one in the non-sacred area (hill) and the other in the sacred area (haram). When he wanted to reprimand his family, he reprimanded them in the non-sacred area. It was said to him, and he said: "We used to narrate that among deviation therein is that a man says: 'No, by Allah,' and 'Yes, by Allah.'"

The eighth, and it is the saying of the muhaqqiqun (verifiers): that deviation with injustice is general to all sins, because whatever is small or great, there is something greater than it in the rest of the places. So much so that Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) said: If a man in 'Aden intended to commit an evil deed at the House, Allah would make him taste a painful punishment. And Mujahid said: Evil deeds are multiplied therein as good deeds are multiplied. If it is said: How can this be said, while His saying ﴿We will make him taste a painful punishment﴾ is not appropriate for all sins? We say: We do not concede that, for every punishment is painful, except that its degrees differ according to the differing of the sin.

The third issue: The "bi" in His saying ﴿bi-ilhad﴾ has two views. The first, which is the preferable one and the choice of the author of al-Kashshaf, is that His saying ﴿bi-ilhadin bi-zulm﴾ comprises two synonymous circumstantial phrases (hal), and the object of yurid is omitted so as to include every possible object, as if He said: "Whoever intends therein any intention, deviating from the course, as a wrongdoer, We will make him taste a painful punishment." That means: the obligation upon whoever is therein is to restrain himself and to follow the path of rectitude and justice in everything he intends and purposes. The second: Abu 'Ubaydah said: Its figurative sense is: "whoever intends therein deviation," and the "ba'" is one of the superfluous particles.

The fourth issue: Since ilhad carries the meaning of inclining from one matter to another, Allah, exalted is He, made clear that what is meant by this ilhad is what is an inclination towards injustice. Therefore He joined injustice with ilhad, because there is no disobedience, great or small, except that it is injustice. For this reason He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, shirk is a great injustice﴾ [Luqman: 13].

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We will make him taste a painful punishment﴾, it is an explanation of the threat, and there are issues concerning it:

The first issue: Whoever says the verse was revealed concerning Ibn Khatal says: What is meant by the punishment is that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) killed him on the day of the Conquest. There is no reason for restricting it when generalisation is possible. Rather, what must be meant is the punishment in the Hereafter, because it is among the greatest of what one is threatened with.

The second issue: This verse indicates that a person deserves punishment by his intention to commit injustice, just as he deserves it for the action of his limbs.

[Page 24]

The third issue: They mentioned two views regarding the predicate of inna mentioned at the beginning of the verse. The first: The estimation is: "Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar [others], and whoever intends therein deviation - We will make him taste a punishment," so it refers to both sentences. The second: that it is omitted, because the answer of the conditional clause indicates it. Its estimation is: "Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar [others] from the Sacred Mosque - We will make them taste a painful punishment." And everyone who commits a sin therein is likewise.

﴿And [remember] when We settled Abraham in the place of the House, [saying]: "Do not associate anything with Me, and purify My House for those who circumambulate it, and those who stand [in prayer], and those who bow and prostrate."﴾ ﴿And proclaim to the people the Hajj; they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel, coming from every deep mountain pass.﴾ ﴿That they may witness benefits for themselves and mention the name of Allah on known days over the provision He has given them of livestock animals. So eat from them and feed the miserable, the poor.﴾ ﴿Then let them complete their rites, fulfil their vows, and circumambulate the Ancient House.﴾

Know that His saying ﴿وإذْ بَوَّأْنا﴾ [And when We settled] means: remember when We made the place of the House a *mubāʾah* (a dwelling place, i.e., a place of return) for Abraham, that is, a place to which he returns for its upkeep and worship. He had lifted the House to the heavens during the time of the Flood, and it was made of red ruby. Allah, exalted is He, informed Abraham, peace be upon him, of its place by means of a wind He sent, which uncovered what was around it, so he built it on its original foundation. It is also said that He commanded Abraham to go to the site of the House and build it. He set out, but its place was hidden from him. So Allah, exalted is He, sent a cloud equal in length and breadth to the Sacred House, and in it was a head that spoke, having a tongue and two eyes. It said: "O Abraham, build upon my measure and in alignment with me." So he began the construction, and the cloud departed. Here there are several questions:

The first question: There is no doubt that *an* (أنْ) is the explanatory particle (*al-mufassirah*, the particle that explains what precedes it). How, then, can the prohibition of associating partners and the command to purify the House be an explanation of *tabwiʾah* (settling)? The answer: when He, glorified is He, said, "We made the House a place of return for Abraham," it was as if it were asked: what is meant by the House being a place of return for him? It was answered that its meaning is that he should be, in his heart, one who affirms the Lord of the House as free of any partner or equal, and, in his body, occupied with cleansing the House of idols and images.

The second question: Since Abraham did not associate anything with Allah, how could he say, "Do not associate with Me"? The answer: the meaning is, do not make a partner for Me in worship, and do not make any other aim a partner with Me in the building of the House.

The third question: The House had not been inhabited before that, so how did He say, "purify My House"? The answer: perhaps that place was a wasteland, and people used to throw filth there. So Abraham was commanded to build the House in that place and to purify it of filth. But it is also possible that it was inhabited, and they had placed idols in it, so Allah, exalted is He, commanded him to demolish that structure and erect a new one; and that is the purification from idols. Or it may be said: the meaning is that after you build it, purify it from whatever is not fitting, such as shirk and false speech.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿لِلطّائِفِينَ والقائِمِينَ﴾ [for those who circumambulate and those who stand], Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "*Al-ṭāʾifīn*" means those who circumambulate the House from among non-people of Makkah; "*al-qāʾimīn*" means those who reside there; "*al-rukkaʿ al-sujūd*" means those who pray among all of them. Others said: "*al-qāʾimūn*" are those who pray, because the one who prays must, in his prayer, combine standing, bowing, and prostration. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 22, verse 27:

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And proclaim to the people the pilgrimage (ḥajj)﴾, there are several issues concerning it:

The first issue: Ibn Muḥaysin read (wa-ādhin), meaning "inform" (aʿlim).

The second issue: Concerning the one commanded, there are two opinions.

The first, which most of the exegetes hold, is that he is Ibrahim, peace be upon him. They said: when Ibrahim, peace be upon him, finished building the House, the Glorified said: ﴿And proclaim to the people the pilgrimage﴾. He said: "My Lord, and how will my voice reach [them]?" He said: "Upon you is the proclamation, and upon Me is the delivery." So Ibrahim, peace be upon him, climbed al-Safa, and in another narration Abu Qubays, and in another narration upon the Maqam. Ibrahim said: "How shall I say it?" Jibril, peace be upon him, said: "Say: Labbayka Allahumma labbayk." So he was the first to make the talbiyah. In another narration, he ascended al-Safa and said: "O people, indeed God has prescribed for you the pilgrimage to the Ancient House," and it reached what was between heaven and earth, so nothing remained that heard his voice except that it answered, saying: "Labbayka Allahumma labbayk." In another narration: "Indeed God calls you to the pilgrimage to the Sacred House, that He may reward you with it Paradise and bring you out of the Fire," so on that day there answered him whoever was in the loins of men and the wombs of women, and everything that his voice reached, of stone, tree, clay, mound or dust. Mujahid said: "No one performs the pilgrimage, and no one will perform it until the Hour arises, except that he has been made to hear that call. Whoever answered once performs the pilgrimage once, and whoever answered twice or more, [performs] the pilgrimage twice or more according to that measure."

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, that he said: "When Ibrahim was commanded to proclaim, the mountains humbled themselves before him, lowered themselves, and the towns were raised up for him."

The judge ʿAbd al-Jabbar said: "Their saying that the rock and clay answered him is remote, because informing is only for one who is commanded to the pilgrimage, not for inanimate objects. As for those from east and west who hear his call, it is not impossible, if God Most High empowers them and removes the obstacles, and the like of this may be permissible in the time of the prophets, peace be upon them."

The second opinion: the one commanded by His saying ﴿And proclaim﴾ is Muhammad (ﷺ). This is the saying of al-Hasan and the choice of most of the Muʿtazilah. They argued for it by saying that whatever comes in the Qur'an and can be understood as addressing Muhammad (ﷺ) is more appropriate. His saying previously was ﴿And when We settled for Ibrahim the place of the House﴾ [al-Hajj: 26], i.e., "And mention, O Muhammad, when We settled..." so it has the status of what was mentioned. So when He says ﴿And proclaim﴾, the address returns to him. On this view they mentioned several interpretations of His saying ﴿And proclaim﴾:

One of them: that God Most High commanded Muhammad (ﷺ) to inform the people of the pilgrimage. Second: al-Jubba'i said: God commanded him to announce the talbiyah, so that he informs the people that he is a pilgrim, and they perform the pilgrimage with him. He said: and in His saying ﴿they will come to you﴾ is an indication that the intention is that he perform the pilgrimage so that he may be followed. Third: that it is the beginning of the obligation of the pilgrimage from God Most High upon the Messenger (ﷺ).

As for His saying: ﴿They will come to you on foot and on every lean camel; they will come from every deep mountain pass﴾, there are several issues concerning it:

The first issue: "rijal" are those who walk, singular rajil, like qiyam and qa'im (sic: niyam and na'im). It is also read rujal with a damma on the ra', with the jim light or heavy, and rijal like ʿijal, related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both. His saying ﴿and on every lean camel﴾ means riders. Ḍumur is emaciation (al-huzal): it is said ḍamura yaḍmuru ḍumūran, and the meaning is that the she-camel became lean due to the length of her journey. He said ﴿they will come﴾ referring to the group of camels, which are the lean ones, because His saying ﴿and on every lean camel﴾ means "on lean camels," so the verb was made to agree with the sense of "every." Had he said "yaʾti" following the wording, it would have been correct. It is also read yaʾtūna as an attribute of the men and riders. Al-fajj is the path between two mountains, then it is used for all paths by extension, and al-ʿamīq is the distant. Ibn Masʿud read "maʿīq." It is said: a well deep in its depth (ʿumq) and depth (maʿq).

The second issue: the meaning is: "And proclaim so that they come to you on foot and on every lean camel," i.e., proclaim so that they come to you with these two attributes; or the meaning is: "And proclaim, for they will come to you with these two attributes."

The third issue: God began with mention of those on foot to honor them. Saʿid ibn Jubayr narrated with his chain from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed the mounted pilgrim, for every step his mount takes he has seventy good deeds, and for the one on foot seven hundred good deeds of the good deeds of the Sacred Precinct." It was said: "O Messenger of God, what are the good deeds of the Sacred Precinct?" He said: "A good deed is worth a hundred thousand good deeds."

The fourth issue: He said ﴿they will come to you on foot﴾ because he is the one who proclaims; so whoever comes to Mecca as a pilgrim, it is as though he has come to Ibrahim, since he answers his call.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 22, verses 28–29:

As for His saying: ﴿That they may witness benefits for themselves and mention the name of Allah on known days﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: When He, exalted is He, commanded the Hajj in His saying: ﴿And proclaim to mankind the Hajj﴾, He mentioned the wisdom of that command in His saying: ﴿That they may witness benefits for themselves﴾. The scholars differed concerning these benefits. Some understood them as the benefits of this world, namely that they should trade during the days of Hajj. Others understood them as the benefits of the Hereafter, namely pardon and forgiveness, from Muhammad al-Baqir (peace be upon him). Others understood them as both together, and this is the preferable view.

The second issue: He made "benefits" indefinite (nakira) because He intended benefits特 to this worship, both religious and worldly, that are not found in other acts of worship.

The third issue: He alluded to the slaughter and the sacrifice by mentioning the name of Allah the Exalted, because the people of Islam do not cease to mention His name when they sacrifice and slaughter. In this there is an indication that the essential purpose in what is offered to draw near to Allah the Exalted is that the name of Allah the Exalted be mentioned, and that one should differ from the polytheists in this, for they used to slaughter for the idols (nusub) and images. Muqatil said: "When you slaughter, say: 'In the name of Allah, Allah is the Greatest. O Allah, from You and to You,' and face the qiblah." Al-Kalbi added and said: "Indeed my prayer, my sacrifice, my life and my death are for Allah, Lord of the worlds." Al-Qaffal said: "The one who draws near by it and by shedding its blood is imagined in the form of one who ransoms his own self with something equal to it; so he gives up that sheep in place of his own soul, seeking the pleasure of Allah the Exalted, and acknowledging that his shortcoming deserves his soul."

The fourth issue: Most scholars hold that the known days are the ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah, and the numbered days (al-ma'dudat) are the days of tashriq. This is the view of Mujahid, 'Ata', Qatadah and al-Hasan, and a narration of Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas, and the choice of al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on them. They argued that they are known to the people because of their eagerness to know them, since the time of Hajj is at their end. Then, for the benefits, there are times within the ten that are well known, such as the Day of 'Arafah and the Sacred Mash'ar; likewise the sacrificial animals have a time within them, which is the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-nahr). Ibn 'Abbas said, in a narration of 'Ata': they are the Day of Sacrifice and three days after it. This is the choice of Abu Muslim, who said: "Because they were known to the Arabs after it, and they are the days of sacrifice." This is also the view of Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on them both.

Page 27

As for His saying: ﴿of the grazing livestock (bahimat al-an'am)﴾, the author of al-Kashshaf said: "Bahimah" is indefinite (mubhamah) in every four-legged creature on land and sea, so it was specified by "al-an'am," which are the camels, cattle, sheep and goats.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So eat from them﴾, some people said it is a command of obligation, because the people of the Jahiliyyah did not eat from them, out of haughtiness toward the poor. So He commanded the Muslims to do so, since in it there is opposition to the disbelievers, equality with the poor, and the practice of humility. Most scholars said it is not obligatory. Then the scholars said: whoever offers a gift (hady) or sacrifices, it is good that he eats half and gives half in charity, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So eat from them and feed the miserable, the poor﴾. Some said he eats a third, keeps a third, and gives a third in charity. The school of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, is that eating is recommended and feeding is obligatory; if he feeds all of it, it suffices him, and if he eats all of it, it does not suffice him. This applies to voluntary offerings. As for obligatory ones, such as those due to vows, expiations, and compensations for deficiencies, such as the blood of qiran, the blood of tamattu', the blood of an offense, and the blood of shaving and cutting the hair, then none of it may be eaten.

As for His saying: ﴿And feed the miserable, the poor﴾, there is no doubt that it is a command of obligation. The "miserable" (ba'is) is one who has been struck by distress (bu's), that is, hardship; and the "poor" (faqir) is one whom poverty has weakened, and the word is derived from faqar al-zahr (the spine). Ibn 'Abbas said: The miserable is one whose distress is evident in his clothing and his face, while the poor is one who is not like that, so his clothing is clean and his face is the face of a rich man.

As for His saying: ﴿Then let them end their unkemptness (tafath)﴾, al-Zajjaj said: "The linguists do not know tafath except from the tafsir." Al-Mubarrad said: "The origin of tafath in the speech of the Arabs is every filth that clings to a person, so it is obligatory for him to remove it." What is meant here is trimming the moustache and nails, plucking the armpit hair, and shaving the pubic hair; and what is meant by "qada'" is removing the tafath. Al-Qaffal said: Nifṭawayh said: "I asked an eloquent Bedouin what is meant by His saying: ﴿Then let them end their tafath﴾? He said: 'I do not interpret the Qur'an, but we say to a man: how unkempt you are, and how filthy you are!'" Then al-Qaffal said: "This is preferable to the view of al-Zajjaj, because the statement of the affirmer is preferred over the statement of the negator."

As for His saying: ﴿And let them fulfil their vows﴾, it is read with the shaddah on the fa'. Then this may include what entering into Hajj made obligatory of the types of rites; and it may be that what is meant is what they made obligatory by vow, which is speech. This latter view is the closer, for when a man performs Hajj or 'umrah he may obligate himself to offerings and other things that Hajj would not have required without his obligating them; so Allah, exalted is He, commanded fulfilling that.

As for His saying: ﴿And let them circumambulate the Ancient House﴾, what is meant is the obligatory tawaf, which is the tawaf of ifadah and ziyarah. As for whether this tawaf is after standing at 'Arafah, stoning the jamarat and shaving, and then whether it is on the Day of Sacrifice or after it, there is detail in this. The House was called "the Ancient House" (al-Bayt al-'Atiq) for several reasons:

One: al-'Atiq means the ancient, because it is the first house placed for mankind, according to al-Hasan. Second: because it was freed (u'tiqa) from the tyrants, for many a tyrant marched toward it to demolish it, but Allah, exalted is He, prevented him; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and the view of Ibn al-Zubayr, and they narrated it from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). When Abrahah targeted it, what was done to him was done. If it is said: then al-Hajjaj gained power over it, the answer is: we say he did not intend to gain power over the House itself; rather 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr had taken refuge in it, so he devised a way to expel him, and then rebuilt it. Third: it was never owned, according to Ibn 'Uyaynah. Fourth: it was freed from drowning, according to Mujahid. Fifth: it is a noble house, from their saying: "'ita¡q of birds and horses" (noble birds and horses).

Know that the lam in liyaqdu, wal-yufu, and walyattawwafu is the lam of command. In the recitation of Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and most readers, these lams are pronounced light (takhfif); in the recitation of Abu 'Amr they are vowelled with a kasrah (tahrik bil-kasr).

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 22, verses 28–29:

As for His saying: ﴿That they may witness benefits for themselves and mention the name of Allah on known days﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: When He, exalted is He, commanded the Hajj in His saying: ﴿And proclaim to mankind the Hajj﴾, He mentioned the wisdom of that command in His saying: ﴿That they may witness benefits for themselves﴾. The scholars differed concerning these benefits. Some understood them as the benefits of this world, namely that they should trade during the days of Hajj. Others understood them as the benefits of the Hereafter, namely pardon and forgiveness, from Muhammad al-Baqir (peace be upon him). Others understood them as both together, and this is the preferable view.

The second issue: He made "benefits" indefinite (nakira) because He intended benefits特 to this worship, both religious and worldly, that are not found in other acts of worship.

The third issue: He alluded to the slaughter and the sacrifice by mentioning the name of Allah the Exalted, because the people of Islam do not cease to mention His name when they sacrifice and slaughter. In this there is an indication that the essential purpose in what is offered to draw near to Allah the Exalted is that the name of Allah the Exalted be mentioned, and that one should differ from the polytheists in this, for they used to slaughter for the idols (nusub) and images. Muqatil said: "When you slaughter, say: 'In the name of Allah, Allah is the Greatest. O Allah, from You and to You,' and face the qiblah." Al-Kalbi added and said: "Indeed my prayer, my sacrifice, my life and my death are for Allah, Lord of the worlds." Al-Qaffal said: "The one who draws near by it and by shedding its blood is imagined in the form of one who ransoms his own self with something equal to it; so he gives up that sheep in place of his own soul, seeking the pleasure of Allah the Exalted, and acknowledging that his shortcoming deserves his soul."

The fourth issue: Most scholars hold that the known days are the ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah, and the numbered days (al-ma'dudat) are the days of tashriq. This is the view of Mujahid, 'Ata', Qatadah and al-Hasan, and a narration of Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas, and the choice of al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on them. They argued that they are known to the people because of their eagerness to know them, since the time of Hajj is at their end. Then, for the benefits, there are times within the ten that are well known, such as the Day of 'Arafah and the Sacred Mash'ar; likewise the sacrificial animals have a time within them, which is the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-nahr). Ibn 'Abbas said, in a narration of 'Ata': they are the Day of Sacrifice and three days after it. This is the choice of Abu Muslim, who said: "Because they were known to the Arabs after it, and they are the days of sacrifice." This is also the view of Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on them both.

Page 27

As for His saying: ﴿of the grazing livestock (bahimat al-an'am)﴾, the author of al-Kashshaf said: "Bahimah" is indefinite (mubhamah) in every four-legged creature on land and sea, so it was specified by "al-an'am," which are the camels, cattle, sheep and goats.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So eat from them﴾, some people said it is a command of obligation, because the people of the Jahiliyyah did not eat from them, out of haughtiness toward the poor. So He commanded the Muslims to do so, since in it there is opposition to the disbelievers, equality with the poor, and the practice of humility. Most scholars said it is not obligatory. Then the scholars said: whoever offers a gift (hady) or sacrifices, it is good that he eats half and gives half in charity, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So eat from them and feed the miserable, the poor﴾. Some said he eats a third, keeps a third, and gives a third in charity. The school of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, is that eating is recommended and feeding is obligatory; if he feeds all of it, it suffices him, and if he eats all of it, it does not suffice him. This applies to voluntary offerings. As for obligatory ones, such as those due to vows, expiations, and compensations for deficiencies, such as the blood of qiran, the blood of tamattu', the blood of an offense, and the blood of shaving and cutting the hair, then none of it may be eaten.

As for His saying: ﴿And feed the miserable, the poor﴾, there is no doubt that it is a command of obligation. The "miserable" (ba'is) is one who has been struck by distress (bu's), that is, hardship; and the "poor" (faqir) is one whom poverty has weakened, and the word is derived from faqar al-zahr (the spine). Ibn 'Abbas said: The miserable is one whose distress is evident in his clothing and his face, while the poor is one who is not like that, so his clothing is clean and his face is the face of a rich man.

As for His saying: ﴿Then let them end their unkemptness (tafath)﴾, al-Zajjaj said: "The linguists do not know tafath except from the tafsir." Al-Mubarrad said: "The origin of tafath in the speech of the Arabs is every filth that clings to a person, so it is obligatory for him to remove it." What is meant here is trimming the moustache and nails, plucking the armpit hair, and shaving the pubic hair; and what is meant by "qada'" is removing the tafath. Al-Qaffal said: Nifṭawayh said: "I asked an eloquent Bedouin what is meant by His saying: ﴿Then let them end their tafath﴾? He said: 'I do not interpret the Qur'an, but we say to a man: how unkempt you are, and how filthy you are!'" Then al-Qaffal said: "This is preferable to the view of al-Zajjaj, because the statement of the affirmer is preferred over the statement of the negator."

As for His saying: ﴿And let them fulfil their vows﴾, it is read with the shaddah on the fa'. Then this may include what entering into Hajj made obligatory of the types of rites; and it may be that what is meant is what they made obligatory by vow, which is speech. This latter view is the closer, for when a man performs Hajj or 'umrah he may obligate himself to offerings and other things that Hajj would not have required without his obligating them; so Allah, exalted is He, commanded fulfilling that.

As for His saying: ﴿And let them circumambulate the Ancient House﴾, what is meant is the obligatory tawaf, which is the tawaf of ifadah and ziyarah. As for whether this tawaf is after standing at 'Arafah, stoning the jamarat and shaving, and then whether it is on the Day of Sacrifice or after it, there is detail in this. The House was called "the Ancient House" (al-Bayt al-'Atiq) for several reasons:

One: al-'Atiq means the ancient, because it is the first house placed for mankind, according to al-Hasan. Second: because it was freed (u'tiqa) from the tyrants, for many a tyrant marched toward it to demolish it, but Allah, exalted is He, prevented him; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and the view of Ibn al-Zubayr, and they narrated it from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). When Abrahah targeted it, what was done to him was done. If it is said: then al-Hajjaj gained power over it, the answer is: we say he did not intend to gain power over the House itself; rather 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr had taken refuge in it, so he devised a way to expel him, and then rebuilt it. Third: it was never owned, according to Ibn 'Uyaynah. Fourth: it was freed from drowning, according to Mujahid. Fifth: it is a noble house, from their saying: "'ita¡q of birds and horses" (noble birds and horses).

Know that the lam in liyaqdu, wal-yufu, and walyattawwafu is the lam of command. In the recitation of Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and most readers, these lams are pronounced light (takhfif); in the recitation of Abu 'Amr they are vowelled with a kasrah (tahrik bil-kasr).

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 22, verses 30–32:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿That [is so]. And whoever honours the sacred rites of Allah, it is better for him with his Lord. And the cattle have been made lawful for you, except what is recited to you [as forbidden]. So avoid the abomination of the idols, and avoid the word of falsehood,﴾ ﴿turning to Allah in pure faith, not associating anything with Him. And whoever associates partners with Allah, it is as if he had fallen from the sky and the birds had snatched him, or the wind had swept him away to a distant place.﴾ ﴿That [is so]. And whoever honours the symbols of Allah, indeed it is from the piety of the hearts.﴾

The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: "Dhalika" (that) is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "the matter and the affair is that," just as a writer introduces a passage of his speech on some topic, and when he wishes to turn to another topic he says, "This, and it was such-and-such." Ḥurma (sanctity) is that which must not be violated. All that Allah has imposed on the person with this quality, from the rites of the Hajj and others, may be general to all of His obligations, and it may be specific to what relates to the Hajj. From Zayd ibn Aslam: the sacred things are five: the Sacred House (al-Ka'ba al-Ḥarām), the Sacred Mosque, the Sacred Land, the Sacred Month, and the Sacred Monument (al-Mash'ar al-Ḥarām). The theologians (al-Mutakallimun) said: supererogatory acts (nawafil) are not included among the sacred things of Allah. ﴿It is better for him with his Lord﴾: that is, honouring them is good for him, because he knows that it is obligatory to uphold and preserve them. His saying ﴿with his Lord﴾ indicates a reward that is stored up, because one does not say "with his Lord" concerning a good that has already been obtained. Al-Asamm said: ﴿it is better for him﴾ than neglecting this.

Then He returned to explaining the ruling of the Hajj, saying: ﴿And the cattle have been made lawful for you﴾. It could have been thought that since the state of iḥrām prohibits hunting and other things, the cattle would also be prohibited. So Allah made clear that iḥrām does not affect them, and they are permitted. He excepted from this what is recited in the Book of Allah of the prohibited livestock, which is mentioned in Surah al-Ma'ida, namely His saying: ﴿other than those who hunt game while you are in the state of iḥrām﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 1], and His saying: ﴿Prohibited to you are﴾ [al-Nisa': 23], and His saying: ﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned﴾ [al-An'am: 121].

Then, when He, glorified is He, urged the honouring of His sacred things and praised those who honour them, He followed this with the command to avoid idols and false speech, because the Oneness of Allah and truthfulness of speech are the greatest of goods. He combined associating partners and false speech in one thread because associating partners is a kind of falsehood: the polytheist claims that the idol deserves worship. It is as if He said: avoid the worship of idols, which is the head of falsehood, and avoid false speech entirely, and do not approach any of it at all, given its extreme ugliness and vileness. And what do you think of something of its kind, the worship of idols? He called the idols "rijs" (abomination), not because of impurity, but because the obligation to avoid them is more emphatic than the obligation to avoid the abomination, and because worshipping them is greater than being soiled by impurities.

Then al-Asamm said: He described them with this only because their custom in acts of drawing near (to their gods) was to deliberately make blood fall upon them. This is far-fetched. It was also said that He described them with this to belittle and despise them, and this is closer to the truth. His saying ﴿of the idols﴾ is an explanation of "rijs" and a specification of it, like the saying "I have twenty of dirhams." Because "rijs," due to its ambiguity, applies to everything, it is as if He said: avoid the abomination which is the idols. The intended meaning is not that some of them are not like that.

"Al-zūr" (falsehood) derives from "al-zawr" and "al-izwirār," which means deviation, just as "al-ifk" (lie) derives from "afakahu" when he turned it away. The exegetes have mentioned several meanings of "the word of falsehood":
First: their saying, "This is lawful and this is forbidden," and similar fabrications.
Second: false testimony. It is reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he prayed the dawn prayer, and when he finished the salutation, he stood up, faced the people, and said: "The testimony of falsehood is equal to associating partners with Allah," and then recited this verse.
Third: lying and slander.
Fourth: the saying of the people of the Jahiliyya in their talbiya: "Here I am, O Allah, no partner for You, except a partner who is Yours, You own him and what he owns."

* * *

As for His saying ﴿turning to Allah (ḥunafā' li-Llāh)﴾: the explanation of this has already been mentioned, and that it means steadfastness according to some, and inclination to the truth according to others. The intended meaning here is what has been said: sincerity (al-ikhlāṣ). It is as if He said: hold fast to these matters that I have commanded and forbidden, in the manner of worshipping Allah alone, not in the manner of associating anything other than Allah with Him. Therefore He said: ﴿not associating [anything] with Him﴾. This indicates that it is obligatory on the one who is accountable that he intend sincerity in whatever act of worship he performs. Then Allah, exalted is He, gave two examples of disbelief, with no addition to them, to show that the disbeliever harms himself and gains nothing from himself. This is His saying: ﴿And whoever associates partners with Allah, it is as if he had fallen from the sky and the birds had snatched him, or the wind had swept him away to a distant place.﴾

The author of al-Kashshaf said: If this is a compound simile (tashbīh murakkab), then it is as if it were said: whoever associates partners with Allah has destroyed himself with a destruction beyond which there is no destruction, by depicting his state as the state of one who has fallen from the sky, and the birds have snatched him, scattering his parts into their crops, or the wind has swept him until it hurled him into some far-off ruin. If it is a separate simile (tashbīh mufarraq), then faith is likened in its loftiness to the sky; the one who abandoned faith and associated partners with Allah is like the one who has fallen from the sky; the desires that scatter his thoughts are like the snatching birds; and Satan, who casts him into the valley of misguidance, is like the wind that hurls what it has swept into various abysses.

It is read with a kasra on the kha' and ṭā' and with a kasra on the fā' as well, and this is the reading of al-Hasan. Its original form is "takhṭafuhu." It is also read "al-riyāḥ" (the winds).

Then He, glorified is He, emphasised what preceded, saying: ﴿That [is so]. And whoever honours the symbols of Allah﴾. The scholars differed: some said it includes every act of worship; some said it is the rites of the Hajj; and some said the intended meaning is specifically the sacrificial animals (hady). The original meaning of "sha'ā'ir" (symbols) is the markers by which a thing is recognised. If we interpret "sha'ā'ir" as the sacrificial animals, then honouring them is in two ways:

First: that he chooses them large in body, beautiful, stout, fat, and of high price, and that he refrains from haggling over their purchase. They used to pay high prices for three things and disliked haggling over them: the hady, the udhiyya (sacrificial animal), and the slave. It is reported from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he gave as a gift a noble she-camel which was requested from him for three hundred dinars. He asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to let him sell it and buy with its price camels for sacrifice, but he forbade him from that and said: "Rather, give it as a gift." And the Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave as gifts one hundred camels, among them a camel belonging to Abu Jahl with a gold ring in its nose.

The second way of honouring the symbols of Allah, exalted is He, is that he believes that obeying Allah by drawing near to Him through them and sending them to His honoured House is a great matter, which must be celebrated and hastened to: ﴿indeed it is from the piety of the hearts﴾, that is: indeed honouring them is from the actions of those with piety of the hearts. The words (in the original) have been omitted, and the meaning cannot be correct without supplying them, because there must be a returning pronoun in the apodosis to the one it is connected with. The hearts are mentioned because the hypocrite may show piety outwardly, but since his heart is empty of it, he is certainly not diligent in performing acts of obedience. As for the sincere person in whose heart piety is firmly established, he strives greatly in performing acts of obedience with sincerity.

It was also said that He described them with this to belittle and despise them, and this is closer to the truth. His saying ﴿of the idols﴾ is an explanation of "rijs" and a specification of it, like the saying "I have twenty of dirhams." Because "rijs," due to its ambiguity, applies to everything, it is as if He said: avoid the abomination which is the idols. The intended meaning is not that some of them are not like that.

"Al-zūr" (falsehood) derives from "al-zawr" and "al-izwirār," which means deviation, just as "al-ifk" (lie) derives from "afakahu" when he turned it away. The exegetes have mentioned several meanings of "the word of falsehood":
First: their saying, "This is lawful and this is forbidden," and similar fabrications.
Second: false testimony. It is reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he prayed the dawn prayer, and when he finished the salutation, he stood up, faced the people, and said: "The testimony of falsehood is equal to associating partners with Allah," and then recited this verse.
Third: lying and slander.
Fourth: the saying of the people of the Jahiliyya in their talbiya: "Here I am, O Allah, no partner for You, except a partner who is Yours, You own him and what he owns."

* * *

As for His saying ﴿turning to Allah (ḥunafā' li-Llāh)﴾: the explanation of this has already been mentioned, and that it means steadfastness according to some, and inclination to the truth according to others. The intended meaning here is what has been said: sincerity (al-ikhlāṣ). It is as if He said: hold fast to these matters that I have commanded and forbidden, in the manner of worshipping Allah alone, not in the manner of associating anything other than Allah with Him. Therefore He said: ﴿not associating [anything] with Him﴾. This indicates that it is obligatory on the one who is accountable that he intend sincerity in whatever act of worship he performs. Then Allah, exalted is He, gave two examples of disbelief, with no addition to them, to show that the disbeliever harms himself and gains nothing from himself. This is His saying: ﴿And whoever associates partners with Allah, it is as if he had fallen from the sky and the birds had snatched him, or the wind had swept him away to a distant place.﴾

The author of al-Kashshaf said: If this is a compound simile (tashbīh murakkab), then it is as if it were said: whoever associates partners with Allah has destroyed himself with a destruction beyond which there is no destruction, by depicting his state as the state of one who has fallen from the sky, and the birds have snatched him, scattering his parts into their crops, or the wind has swept him until it hurled him into some far-off ruin. If it is a separate simile (tashbīh mufarraq), then faith is likened in its loftiness to the sky; the one who abandoned faith and associated partners with Allah is like the one who has fallen from the sky; the desires that scatter his thoughts are like the snatching birds; and Satan, who casts him into the valley of misguidance, is like the wind that hurls what it has swept into various abysses.

It is read with a kasra on the kha' and ṭā' and with a kasra on the fā' as well, and this is the reading of al-Hasan. Its original form is "takhṭafuhu." It is also read "al-riyāḥ" (the winds).

Then He, glorified is He, emphasised what preceded, saying: ﴿That [is so]. And whoever honours the symbols of Allah﴾. The scholars differed: some said it includes every act of worship; some said it is the rites of the Hajj; and some said the intended meaning is specifically the sacrificial animals (hady). The original meaning of "sha'ā'ir" (symbols) is the markers by which a thing is recognised. If we interpret "sha'ā'ir" as the sacrificial animals, then honouring them is in two ways:

First: that he chooses them large in body, beautiful, stout, fat, and of high price, and that he refrains from haggling over their purchase. They used to pay high prices for three things and disliked haggling over them: the hady, the udhiyya (sacrificial animal), and the slave. It is reported from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he gave as a gift a noble she-camel which was requested from him for three hundred dinars. He asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to let him sell it and buy with its price camels for sacrifice, but he forbade him from that and said: "Rather, give it as a gift." And the Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave as gifts one hundred camels, among them a camel belonging to Abu Jahl with a gold ring in its nose.

The second way of honouring the symbols of Allah, exalted is He, is that he believes that obeying Allah by drawing near to Him through them and sending them to His honoured House is a great matter, which must be celebrated and hastened to: ﴿indeed it is from the piety of the hearts﴾, that is: indeed honouring them is from the actions of those with piety of the hearts. The words (in the original) have been omitted, and the meaning cannot be correct without supplying them, because there must be a returning pronoun in the apodosis to the one it is connected with. The hearts are mentioned because the hypocrite may show piety outwardly, but since his heart is empty of it, he is certainly not diligent in performing acts of obedience. As for the sincere person in whose heart piety is firmly established, he strives greatly in performing acts of obedience with sincerity.

If someone asks: what is the wisdom in Allah, exalted is He, emphasising the slaughter of animals to this extent? The answer is:

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 22, verse 33:

Page 30

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For you there are benefits in them until a specified term; then their place of sacrifice is at the Ancient House﴾ ﴿And for every community We have appointed rites, that they may mention the name of Allah over what He has provided for them of the beast of cattle. Your God is one God, so submit to Him. And give good tidings to the humble﴾ ﴿Those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned, and the patient over what afflicts them, and those who establish prayer and spend from what We have provided for them﴾.

Know that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For you there are benefits in them until a specified term﴾ is only fitting if the rites (sha'a'ir) are taken to mean the sacrificial animals (hady), which have benefits until the time of slaughter (nahr). As for one who takes this to refer to all the obligations, he says: "For you in them", meaning in adhering to them, there are benefits until a term at which the obligation ends. The first is the saying of the majority of the exegetes, and there is no doubt that it is closer. On this view, the benefits are explained as milk, offspring, wool, and riding upon them. As for His saying "until a specified term", there are two opinions. One of them: you may benefit from these animals until you designate them as a sacrificial offering (dahiyyah) and a sacrificial gift (hady). When you do that, you are no longer permitted to benefit from them. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ata', Qatadah and al-Dahhak. Others said: "For you in them", that is, in the camels (budn), there are benefits along with designating them as hady, by riding them if you need to, and drinking their milk if you are compelled to, until a specified term, meaning until you slaughter them. This is the second narration from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, and it is the choice of al-Shafi'i. This view is preferable, because He, exalted is He, said: "For you in them are benefits", that is, in the rites, and they are not called rites before they are called hady. Abu Hurayrah narrated that the Prophet, peace be upon him, passed by a man driving a camel while he was in hardship, and he, peace be upon him, said: "Ride it." He said: "O Messenger of Allah, it is a hady." He said: "Ride it, woe to you." Jabir narrated from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that he said: "Ride the hady with what is reasonable until you find a mount." Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, argued that one does not own its benefits, on the ground that it is not permissible for him to rent it out for riding; had he owned its benefits, he would have had the right to contract a lease upon it, like the benefits of other owned property. This is weak, because the mother of a child (umm al-walad) cannot be sold, yet the owner may benefit from her, so likewise here.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿then their place of sacrifice is at the Ancient House﴾, the meaning is that for you in the sacrificial animals there are many benefits in your worldly life and your religion, and the greatest of these benefits is their place of sacrifice (mahill) at the Ancient House, that is, the obligation of slaughtering them, or the time of the obligation of their slaughter, extends to the House, as in His saying: ﴿an offering reaching the Ka'bah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 95]. In sum, His saying "their place of sacrifice" means the place where their slaughter becomes lawful. As for the Ancient House, what is meant by it is the entire Sacred Precinct (haram), and its evidence is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So let them not approach the Sacred Mosque after this year of theirs﴾ [al-Tawbah: 28], meaning the entire Sacred Precinct. Thus, according to this view, the place of slaughter is all of Makkah, but it is cleansed of blood except at Mina, and Mina is part of Makkah. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Every pass of Makkah is a place of slaughter, and every pass of Mina is a place of slaughter." Al-Qaffal said: this applies specifically to the sacrificial animals that have reached Mina. As for a voluntary offering that perishes before reaching Makkah, its place of slaughter is the place where it is.

﴿And for every community We appointed a rite,﴾ [meaning] that they might mention the name of God... The meaning is: We legislated for every community among the earlier nations, from the time of Abraham, peace be upon him, onward, a form of qurban (sacrificial offering). The reason for this was that they should mention the name of God, exalted are His names, over the rites. What the Arabs used to slaughter for an idol was called al-'atr and al-'atirah, like al-dhabh (the slaughter) and al-dhabihah (the slaughtered animal). The people of Kufa, except 'Asim, read ﻣَﻨْﺴَﻜًﺎ (mansakan) with a kasrah on the sin, while the rest read it with a fatha. The fatha form is a verbal noun meaning al-nusk (worship/rite), and the kasrah form means the place.

As for His saying, ﴿So your God is one God,﴾ there are two views on how the verse is composed:

Abu Muslim said: The essential meaning of mukhbit is one who has entered a khabt of the earth. It is said: akhbata al-rajul when he entered the khabt, just as it is said anjada, ash’ama and atham. As for what befalls them from wrongdoers, patience toward it is not obligatory; rather, if he is able to repel it, he is obliged to repel it, even by fighting. The second is occupation with service.
