**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 22, verse 36:**

God Most High says: ﴿And the camels We have appointed for you as among the symbols of God; in them there is good for you. So mention the name of God over them as they stand in ranks. Then when their sides fall (after slaughter), eat from them and feed the contented one and the beggar. Thus We have subjected them to you, that you may be grateful.﴾ ﴿Neither their flesh nor their blood reaches God, but piety from you reaches Him. Thus He has subjected them to you that you may magnify God for having guided you. And give good news to the good-doers.﴾

Know that God's words ﴿And the camels﴾ raise several issues.

**First issue:** *al-budn* is the plural of *badanah*, as *khushb* is the plural of *khashabah* (wood). It was so called when it was dedicated to the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram) because of the bulk (*ʿizam badanihā*) of its body. Strictly, it refers only to camels. However, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) extended it to cattle when he said: "A camel counts for seven, and a cow counts for seven." Also, God says: ﴿when their sides fall﴾, and this applies specifically to camels, for they are slaughtered standing, not cows. Some people said: *al-budn* means camels and the cows that are offered as a means of drawing near to God during the Hajj and the ʿUmrah, because the name derives from the bulk of the body, so it is preferable to include them. As for sheep, they are not included, even though they are acceptable in sacrificial rites, because they are small in body and so are not called *badanah*.

**Second issue:** al-Hasan read *wa-l-budunа* with two dammas, like *thumur*, the plural of *thamarah* (fruit). Ibn Abi Ishaq read it with two dammas and a doubled nun, according to the pause form. It was also read in the accusative and nominative, like His words: ﴿And the moon—We have determined for it stations﴾ (Yasin 36:39). God knows best.

**Third issue:** If someone says, "It is incumbent upon me to offer a *badanah* to God," may he slaughter it outside Mecca? Abu Hanifa and Muhammad, may God have mercy on both of them, said: it is permissible. Abu Yusuf, may God have mercy on him, said: it is not permissible except in Mecca. They agreed that for one who vows a *hady* (offering), it is obligatory to slaughter it in Mecca. But if he says, "It is incumbent upon me to offer a *jazur* (camel)," he may slaughter it wherever he wishes. Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, said: the *badanah* is in the same position as the *jazur*, so it is permissible for him to slaughter it wherever he wishes, unlike the *hady*, for God says: ﴿as an offering reaching the Kaaba﴾ (al-Ma'idah 5:95), so He made reaching the Kaaba a description of the *hady*. Abu Yusuf, may God have mercy on him, argued from His words: ﴿And the camels We have appointed for you as among the symbols of God﴾. So the name *badanah* indicates that it is an act of drawing near to God, and therefore it is like the name *hady*. Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, replied that not everything whose slaughter is an act of drawing near to God is restricted to the Sacred Precinct, for the *udhiyyah* (sacrifice) is an act of drawing near to God, and it is permissible in all places.

As for God's words ﴿We have appointed for you﴾: know that when He, glorified is He, created the camels and made it obligatory that they be offered during the Hajj, it was permissible for Him to say: ﴿We have appointed for you as among the symbols of God﴾. As for His words ﴿in them there is good for you﴾, the discussion of it is what preceded in His words ﴿in them there are benefits for you﴾ (al-Hajj 22:33). Since His words ﴿in them there is good for you﴾ are in the manner of encouragement, the preferable interpretation is that it refers to reward in the Hereafter. How worthy the intelligent person is of eagerness for something about which God Most High has testified that there is good in it and that there are benefits in it!

As for His words ﴿So mention the name of God over them﴾, there is an ellipsis; the meaning is: mention the name of God over their slaughter. The exegetes said: it is to say at the time of slaughter or sacrifice: "In the name of God, God is greatest. O God, from You and to You." As for His words ﴿ṣawāff﴾ (standing in ranks), the meaning is: standing, having set their forelegs and hind legs in position. It was also read *ṣawāfin*, from *ṣufūn al-faras* (the horse standing on three legs with one hoof raised), which means that it stands on three legs and raises the fourth on the tip of its hoof, because the *badanah* is tied so that one of its forelegs is bound, and so it stands on three. It was also read *ṣawāfiyya*, meaning sincere for the sake of God Most High, that you should not associate anyone with God in the naming over its slaughter, as the polytheists used to do. It is also transmitted from ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd that he read *ṣawāfiyan* with tanwin as a substitute for the vowel letter of pausal form. And from some of them: *ṣawāfiya*, like the saying of the Arabs: "Give the bow to its maker (*bārīhā*)." It is not far-fetched that the wisdom in making them stand in ranks is that their large number becomes visible to observers, so the souls of the needy are strengthened, and drawing near to God by slaughtering them at that time is greater in reward and closer to the manifestation of the proclamation of God's greatness, the elevation of God's name and the symbols of His religion.

As for His words ﴿when their sides fall﴾: know that the falling of the sides is their collapsing onto the ground, from the phrase *wajaba al-ḥā'iṭ wajbatan*, when the wall fell, and *wajabat al-shams wajbatan*, when the sun set. The meaning is: when they fall onto the ground, and that is at the departure of the soul from them. ﴿Then eat from them﴾, and we have already mentioned the disagreement of the scholars about what is permissible to eat from them. ﴿And feed the contented one and the beggar.﴾ *Al-qāniʿ* is the one who asks; it is said: *qanaʿa yaqnaʿu qunūʿan* when he asked. Abu ʿUbayd said: it is the man who is with a group seeking their surplus and asking for their kindness and the like. Al-Farra' said: the second meaning of *al-qāniʿ* is the one who does not ask, from *al-qanāʿah* (contentment); it is said: *qanaʿa yaqnaʿu qanāʿatan* when he is pleased with what has been apportioned to him and abandons asking. As for *al-muʿtarr*, it was said: it is the one who presents himself without asking, and it was said: it is the one who presents himself by asking. Al-Azhari said: Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: it is said *ʿaraw-ta fulānan* and *aʿrartahu* and *ʿarawtahu* and *iʿtaraytahu* when you come to him seeking his kindness and the like. Abu ʿUbayd said: the closer meaning is that *al-qāniʿ* is the one who is content with what is given to him without asking or insistence, while *al-muʿtarr* is the one who presents himself, seeks, and comes to them from time to time, so he does what indicates that he is never content with what is given to him. Al-Hasan read *wal-muʿtarri* and Abu Rajaʾ read *al-qanaʿ*, which is the one who is content and nothing more. It is said: *qanaʿa fahuwa qanaʿun wa-qāniʿ*.

As for His words ﴿Thus We have subjected them to you﴾, the meaning is that they are larger, greater and stronger than beasts of prey and other things over which we cannot gain control. God made camels and cattle with the attribute by which we are able to direct them as we wish. That is a great blessing from God Most High in religion and in this world. Then, after God, may He be exalted, had explained this blessing, He said after it: ﴿that you may be grateful﴾, and the meaning is: so that you may give thanks.

The Mu'tazila said: this indicates that He, glorified is He, desired from all of them that they be grateful, and this indicates that He desires everything He commanded from those who obey and those who disobey. This is not as Ahl al-Sunna say, that He Most High only desired this from those known to obey. The discussion of this has preceded more than once.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 22, verse 37:

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It is not their flesh nor their blood that reaches Allah, but it is piety from you that reaches Him﴾, there are several issues concerning it.

The first issue: Since it was the custom of the Jahiliyyah, as is related concerning sacrifice, that they would smear the idol and the walls of the Ka'bah with its blood and flesh, Exalted is He explained what the purpose of slaughter is, saying: ﴿It is not their flesh nor their blood that reaches Allah, but it is piety from you that reaches Him﴾. So He made clear that what reaches Him, Exalted is He, and ascends to Him from the act of the one who draws near (al-mahdi), from his speech, his slaughter and what resembles them of his obligations, is the piety of Allah, not the very flesh and blood. And it is known that none of things is described as reaching Him, glorified is He. Therefore what is meant is that this reaches the place where it is recorded, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿To Him ascends the good word﴾ [Fatir: 10].

The second issue: The Mu'tazilah said: this verse indicates several matters:

The first of them: that what a person benefits from is his action, not the body whose slaughter benefits him.

The second: that He, glorified is He, is free of need of all that, and what is meant is that the servant should strive in carrying out His commands.

The third: that since He did not benefit from the bodies, which are flesh and blood, and benefited from their piety, it is necessary that their piety be an act; otherwise their piety would be in the position of flesh and blood.

The fourth: that since He made acceptance conditional upon piety, and the perpetrator of a major sin is not pious, it is necessary that his deed not be accepted and that he has no reward. The answer: as for the first two, they are correct; as for the third, it is countered by the motive and knowledge; as for the fourth, the perpetrator of a major sin, although he is not pious absolutely, is nevertheless pious regarding what he does of obedience done sincerely, so his obedience must be accepted. At this point the verse turns into an argument against them.

The third issue: All of them recited "yanāla Allāha" and "yanāluhu" with the ya', except Ya'qub, who read both with the ta' (tā'). Whoever made it feminine has referred it to the wording, and whoever made it masculine did so because of the intervening element between the noun and the verb. Then He said: ﴿Thus He subjected them to you﴾. The meaning is that He subjected them in this way so that you may magnify Allah, which is glorification, by what we do at the slaughter and before it and after it, according to what He guided us to, pointed us to, and made clear to us. Then He said after it, in the form of a promise to whoever complies with His command: ﴿And give good tidings to the doers of good﴾, as He said before: ﴿And give good tidings to the humble﴾. The muhsin (doer of good) is one who does what is good of deeds and holds fast to it, so he becomes a benefactor to himself by securing the reward for it.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Surely Allah defends those who believe. Surely Allah does not love every treacherous ingrate.﴾ ﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against, because they have been wronged. And surely Allah is able to give them victory.﴾ ﴿Those who have been driven from their homes without right, only because they say, "Our Lord is Allah." And were it not that Allah repels some people by means of others, monasteries, churches, synagogues and mosques, in which the name of Allah is much mentioned, would surely have been demolished. And Allah will surely help those who help Him. Surely Allah is Strong, Mighty.﴾ ﴿Those who, if We establish them in the land, establish the prayer, give the zakat, enjoin what is good and forbid what is evil. And to Allah belongs the outcome of affairs.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, explained what the Hajj requires, its rites, and the benefits in this world and the Hereafter that it contains, and since we have already mentioned that the disbelievers had barred the believers (from the Sacred Mosque), He followed this with an explanation of what removes the barring and what secures the ability to perform the Hajj. So He said: ﴿Surely Allah defends those who believe.﴾ On this there are several issues:

The first issue: Abu Ja'far, Shayba and Nafi' read *yudafi'u* (with the alif, "defends") and likewise *wa-law la daf'u Allah* (with the alif). Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read both without alif. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and 'Asim read *inna Allaha yudafi'u* with the alif, but *wa-law la daf'u* without the alif. As for one who reads *yudafi'u*, its meaning is that He exaggerates in repelling (harm) from them. Al-Khalil (ibn Ahmad) said: It is said, "Allah repelled the disliked thing from you, *daf'an*, and He defended you, *difa'an*," and *al-difa'* is the better of the two.

The second issue: He mentioned *Surely Allah defends those who believe* without mentioning what He repels, so that it would be more majestic, greater and more comprehensive. In reality, He defends them from the violence of the polytheists. Therefore He said after it, ﴿Surely Allah does not love every treacherous ingrate﴾, thereby indicating that He defends the believers against the schemes of one who has this attribute.

The third issue: Muqatil said: Surely Allah defends the Meccan disbelievers' (harm) from those among the believers who were in Mecca. This was when He commanded the believers to refrain from the Meccan disbelievers before the Hijra (migration), when they harmed them. So they asked the Prophet ﷺ for permission to kill them secretly, and he forbade them.

The fourth issue: This verse is a good news to the believers of their being made superior over the disbelievers and of their being protected from their evils. It is like His saying: ﴿They will not harm you except with a little annoyance﴾ [Al-Imran: 111], and His saying: ﴿Surely We help Our messengers and those who believe﴾ [Ghafir: 51], and He said: ﴿Surely they are the ones who will be helped﴾ [As-Saffat: 172], and ﴿And another (favour) you love: help from Allah and a near victory﴾ [As-Saff: 13].

Its parallel is His saying: ﴿Do not betray Allah and the Messenger, nor betray your trusts﴾ [Al-Anfal: 27]. Muqatil said: They acknowledged the Creator but worshipped other than Him. So what betrayal is greater than this?

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 22, verses 39–41:

As for His words, ﴿Permission is given to those who are being fought, because they have been wronged﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: The people of Madinah, the people of Basra, and Asim in the transmission of Hafs read ”أُذِنَ“ (udhina) with a ḍammah on the alif, while the rest read it with a fatḥah (adhina), meaning: Allah has permitted them to fight. The people of Madinah and Asim read ”يُقاتَلُونَ“ (yuqatalūna) with a fatḥah on the tā’, while Ibn Kathir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read ”أذِنَ“ with a fatḥah on the alif and ”يُقاتِلُونَ“ (yuqatilūna) with a kasrah on the tā’. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: It means that Allah has permitted those who are eager to fight the polytheists in the future. As for the one who reads with a fatḥah on the tā’, the implied meaning is: permission has been given to those who are being fought to engage in fighting.

The second issue: There is an elided element in the verse. The implied meaning is: permission has been given to those who are being fought to fight, so the object of the permission was omitted because ”يُقاتَلُونَ“ indicates it.

As for His words, ﴿because they have been wronged﴾, the meaning is that they were permitted to fight because they had been wronged. They were the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The polytheists of Makkah were harming them with severe harm, and they would come to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from among those who had been beaten and wounded, complaining of their oppression to him. He would say to them: "Be patient, for I have not been commanded to fight until I emigrate." Then Allah revealed this verse, and it is the first verse in which permission to fight was given, after fighting had been forbidden in some seventy-odd verses. It was also said: It was revealed concerning a people who went out as emigrants, and the polytheists of Makkah intercepted them, so permission was given to fight them.

As for His words, ﴿And indeed, Allah is able to give them victory﴾, this is a promise from Him, the Exalted, of their victory, just as a person says to another: "If you obey me, I am able to reward you." He does not mean by this capability alone, but intends that He will certainly do that.

* * *

As for His words, the Exalted, ﴿those who have been expelled from their homes without right﴾, know that when He, the Exalted, explained that they were given permission to fight only because they had been wronged, He clarified that wrong by His words: ﴿those who have been expelled from their homes without right, except that they say, "Our Lord is Allah."﴾ So the Exalted explained their wrongdoing toward them in two respects:

The first: that they expelled them from their homes.

The second: that they expelled them because they said: ﴿Our Lord is Allah.﴾ Each of the two respects is a grave form of wrongdoing. If it is asked: How can ﴿Our Lord is Allah﴾ be an exception from ”without right,” when it is itself something right? We say: The meaning of the sentence is that they were expelled without any cause other than monotheism, which ought to be the cause for acknowledgment and empowerment, not the cause for expulsion and banishment. A similar verse is: ﴿Do you resent us only because we believed in Allah?﴾ Then, by His words: ﴿And were it not that Allah checks some people by means of others, there would have been demolished﴾, the Glorified explained that His custom, may His majesty be exalted, is to preserve His religion by this means. Nafi' read ”لَهُدِمَتْ“ (lahudimat) with light emphasis, while the rest read it with doubled emphasis (lahuddimat). Here there are several questions:

The first question: What is meant by this checking which He attributed to Himself? The answer: It is His permission to the people of His religion to strive against the disbelievers. It is as if He said, the Exalted: "And were it not for Allah's checking the people of polytheism by means of the believers, by permitting them to strive and by giving them victory over their enemies, the people of polytheism would have overpowered the people of the (other) religions and would have rendered inoperative the places of worship they were building." But He repelled this harm from them by commanding the fighting of the enemies of the religion, so that the people of the religion might devote themselves to worship and to building houses for it. For this reason He mentioned the monasteries, the churches, and the prayers, even though they belong to non-Muslims. The commentators mentioned other aspects:

The first: al-Kalbi said: Allah repels by means of the prophets from the believers, and by means of the fighters from those who sit back from jihad.
The second: Abu al-Jawza' narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: Allah repels by means of the good person the evil of the evildoer, by means of the one who prays the one who does not pray, by means of the one who gives charity the one who does not give charity, and by means of the one who performs Hajj the one who does not perform Hajj. And from Ibn Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed Allah repels by means of a righteous Muslim [harm] from a hundred people of his household and his neighbors," then he recited this verse.
The third: al-Dahhak said, from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: He repels by means of the religion of Islam and its people [harm] from the people of the dhimmah (protected non-Muslims).
The fourth: Mujahid said: He repels [loss] from rights by means of witnesses, and [loss] from lives by means of retaliation (qisas).

* * *

The second question: Why did Allah combine the places of worship of the Jews and the Christians with the places of worship of the Muslims? The answer: Concerning what you asked about, they differed in several ways:

The first: al-Hasan said: What is meant by these places is all the places of the believers, even though the expressions for them differ.
The second: the statement of al-Zajjaj: "And were it not that Allah checks some people by means of others, there would have been demolished, in the law of every prophet, the place where prayer is performed. So were it not for that checking, there would have been demolished, in the time of Moses, the churches in which they prayed according to his law, and in the time of Jesus the monasteries, and in the time of our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) the mosques. Accordingly, this protection was extended to them only when they were upon the truth, before distortion and before abrogation."
The third: Rather, what is meant is that these monasteries would have been demolished in the days of the Messenger (ﷺ), because in any case the remembrance of Allah, the Exalted, takes place in them, so they are not on the same footing as the worship of idols.

* * *

The third question: What are the monasteries (ṣawāmi'), the churches (biya'), the prayers (ṣalawāt), and the mosques? The answer: They gave several interpretations:

The first: The monasteries are for the Christians, the churches for the Jews, the prayers for the Sabians, and the mosques for the Muslims, according to Abu al-Aliyah, may Allah be pleased with him.

The second: The monasteries are for the Christians, namely those they built in the deserts; the churches are also for them, namely those they build in towns; and the prayers are for the Jews. Al-Zajjaj said: In Hebrew it is ṣalūtā.

The third: The monasteries are for the Sabians, the churches for the Christians, and the prayers for the Jews, according to Qatadah.

The fourth: All of them are names for mosques, according to al-Hasan. As for the monasteries, it is because Muslims may also adopt monasteries; as for the churches, this name was applied to mosques by way of comparison; and as for the prayers, the meaning is that were it not for that checking, the prayers would have been cut off and the mosques would have been ruined.

* * *

The fourth question: How can prayers be demolished, especially according to the interpretation of those who understood it as the prayer of the Muslims? The answer: There are several respects:

The first: What is meant by demolishing a prayer is its invalidation and the destruction of the one who performs it, like the saying "So-and-so demolished so-and-so's kindness" when he met it with ingratitude instead of gratitude.
The second: Rather, what is meant is the places of the prayers, because that is what can be demolished, like His words: ﴿And ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82], meaning its people.
The third: Since in what was mentioned the majority are things that can be demolished, it is permissible to include with them what cannot be demolished, like the saying "wearing a sword and a spear," even though a spear is not worn.

* * *

The fifth question: Is His words ﴿in which the name of Allah is mentioned much﴾ specific to the mosques, or does it refer to all of them? The answer: Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: It refers to all of them, because Allah, the Exalted, is mentioned much in these places. The more likely view is that it is specific to the mosques, in honor of them, since the remembrance of Allah takes place in them abundantly.

* * *

The sixth question: Why did He mention the monasteries and the churches before the mosques? The answer: Because they are older in existence. It was also said: He placed them later in the mention, as in His words: ﴿And among them is one who is foremost in good deeds by permission of Allah﴾ [Fatir: 32]. And because the first of thought is the last of action. So when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was the best of the messengers and his community the best of communities, they were necessarily the last of them. For this reason he, peace be upon him, said: "We are the last (to come), yet the foremost (in the Hereafter)."

* * *

As for His words, the Exalted, ﴿And Allah will surely help those who help Him﴾, some said: "Those who help Him" means those who accept jihad with acceptance, supporting the religion of Allah, the Exalted. Others said: Rather, what is meant is those who uphold all of His religion. They said this because the help of Allah in the true sense is not valid; what is meant by the help of Allah is the help of His religion, just as it is said of guardianship (wilayah) of Allah and enmity toward Him, similarly. And in His words, ﴿And Allah will surely help those who help Him﴾ is a promise of victory for those who are in this state. The help of Allah, the Exalted, to the servant is that He strengthens him against his enemies until he becomes the victorious one, and that he stands in clarifying the proofs and evidences, and that He assists him in attaining knowledge and acts of obedience. In it there is encouragement toward jihad, since He promised them victory. Then the Exalted explained that He is capable of this victory which He promised to the believers, and that He cannot be prevented from it; and this is the meaning of His words: ﴿Mighty﴾, because the Mighty is the one who cannot be wronged and cannot be prevented from what He wills.

Then, the Glorified and Exalted described those who were given permission to fight in the first verse, saying: ﴿Those who, if We give them authority in the land﴾. What is meant by this authority is sovereignty and the enforceability of command over creation, because what comes first to understanding from His words ﴿if We give them authority in the land﴾ is nothing other than this. Also, if we took it to mean the basic capability, then every servant would be in that state, and then the ordering of the four matters mentioned as the consequence of this would be invalid, because not everyone who is capable of an act performs these things. Having established this, we say: What is meant by them is the emigrants, because His words ﴿those who, if We give them authority﴾ are a description of those mentioned earlier, namely His words ﴿those who have been expelled from their homes﴾, and the Helpers (anṣār) were not expelled from their homes. So the meaning of the verse becomes that Allah, the Exalted, described the emigrants as: if He gives them authority in the land and grants them sovereignty, then they perform the four matters, namely establishing prayer, giving zakat, enjoining what is right, and forbidding what is wrong. But it is established that Allah, the Exalted, gave authority in the land to the four caliphs and granted them sovereignty over it, so it is necessary that they performed these four matters. And since they were enjoining every right and forbidding every wrong, it is necessary that they were upon the truth. Therefore, from this aspect the verse indicates the imamate of the four. It is not permissible to apply the verse to ʿAlī alone, peace be upon him, because the verse is indicative of plurality. And His words ﴿And to Allah belongs the outcome of all matters﴾ indicate that what was mentioned earlier of their sovereignty and dominion is certain to occur. Then, the matters return to Allah, the Exalted, in the end, for He, the Glorified, is the one whose dominion never ceases, and this also confirms what we have said.

It was also said: It was revealed concerning a people who went out as emigrants, and the polytheists of Makkah intercepted them, so permission was given to fight them.

As for His words, ﴿And indeed, Allah is able to give them victory﴾, this is a promise from Him, the Exalted, of their victory, just as a person says to another: "If you obey me, I am able to reward you." He does not mean by this capability alone, but intends that He will certainly do that.

* * *

As for His words, the Exalted, ﴿those who have been expelled from their homes without right﴾, know that when He, the Exalted, explained that they were given permission to fight only because they had been wronged, He clarified that wrong by His words: ﴿those who have been expelled from their homes without right, except that they say, "Our Lord is Allah."﴾ So the Exalted explained their wrongdoing toward them in two respects:

The first: that they expelled them from their homes.

The second: that they expelled them because they said: ﴿Our Lord is Allah.﴾ Each of the two respects is a grave form of wrongdoing. If it is asked: How can ﴿Our Lord is Allah﴾ be an exception from ”without right,” when it is itself something right? We say: The meaning of the sentence is that they were expelled without any cause other than monotheism, which ought to be the cause for acknowledgment and empowerment, not the cause for expulsion and banishment. A similar verse is: ﴿Do you resent us only because we believed in Allah?﴾ Then, by His words: ﴿And were it not that Allah checks some people by means of others, there would have been demolished﴾, the Glorified explained that His custom, may His majesty be exalted, is to preserve His religion by this means. Nafi' read ”لَهُدِمَتْ“ (lahudimat) with light emphasis, while the rest read it with doubled emphasis (lahuddimat). Here there are several questions:

The first question: What is meant by this checking which He attributed to Himself? The answer: It is His permission to the people of His religion to strive against the disbelievers. It is as if He said, the Exalted: "And were it not for Allah's checking the people of polytheism by means of the believers, by permitting them to strive and by giving them victory over their enemies, the people of polytheism would have overpowered the people of the (other) religions and would have rendered inoperative the places of worship they were building." But He repelled this harm from them by commanding the fighting of the enemies of the religion, so that the people of the religion might devote themselves to worship and to building houses for it. For this reason He mentioned the monasteries, the churches, and the prayers, even though they belong to non-Muslims. The commentators mentioned other aspects:

The first: al-Kalbi said: Allah repels by means of the prophets from the believers, and by means of the fighters from those who sit back from jihad.
The second: Abu al-Jawza' narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: Allah repels by means of the good person the evil of the evildoer, by means of the one who prays the one who does not pray, by means of the one who gives charity the one who does not give charity, and by means of the one who performs Hajj the one who does not perform Hajj. And from Ibn Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed Allah repels by means of a righteous Muslim [harm] from a hundred people of his household and his neighbors," then he recited this verse.
The third: al-Dahhak said, from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: He repels by means of the religion of Islam and its people [harm] from the people of the dhimmah (protected non-Muslims).
The fourth: Mujahid said: He repels [loss] from rights by means of witnesses, and [loss] from lives by means of retaliation (qisas).

* * *

The second question: Why did Allah combine the places of worship of the Jews and the Christians with the places of worship of the Muslims? The answer: Concerning what you asked about, they differed in several ways:

The first: al-Hasan said: What is meant by these places is all the places of the believers, even though the expressions for them differ.
The second: the statement of al-Zajjaj: "And were it not that Allah checks some people by means of others, there would have been demolished, in the law of every prophet, the place where prayer is performed. So were it not for that checking, there would have been demolished, in the time of Moses, the churches in which they prayed according to his law, and in the time of Jesus the monasteries, and in the time of our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) the mosques. Accordingly, this protection was extended to them only when they were upon the truth, before distortion and before abrogation."
The third: Rather, what is meant is that these monasteries would have been demolished in the days of the Messenger (ﷺ), because in any case the remembrance of Allah, the Exalted, takes place in them, so they are not on the same footing as the worship of idols.

* * *

The third question: What are the monasteries (ṣawāmi'), the churches (biya'), the prayers (ṣalawāt), and the mosques? The answer: They gave several interpretations:

The first: The monasteries are for the Christians, the churches for the Jews, the prayers for the Sabians, and the mosques for the Muslims, according to Abu al-Aliyah, may Allah be pleased with him.

The second: The monasteries are for the Christians, namely those they built in the deserts; the churches are also for them, namely those they build in towns; and the prayers are for the Jews. Al-Zajjaj said: In Hebrew it is ṣalūtā.

The third: The monasteries are for the Sabians, the churches for the Christians, and the prayers for the Jews, according to Qatadah.

The fourth: All of them are names for mosques, according to al-Hasan. As for the monasteries, it is because Muslims may also adopt monasteries; as for the churches, this name was applied to mosques by way of comparison; and as for the prayers, the meaning is that were it not for that checking, the prayers would have been cut off and the mosques would have been ruined.

* * *

The fourth question: How can prayers be demolished, especially according to the interpretation of those who understood it as the prayer of the Muslims? The answer: There are several respects:

The first: What is meant by demolishing a prayer is its invalidation and the destruction of the one who performs it, like the saying "So-and-so demolished so-and-so's kindness" when he met it with ingratitude instead of gratitude.
The second: Rather, what is meant is the places of the prayers, because that is what can be demolished, like His words: ﴿And ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82], meaning its people.
The third: Since in what was mentioned the majority are things that can be demolished, it is permissible to include with them what cannot be demolished, like the saying "wearing a sword and a spear," even though a spear is not worn.

* * *

The fifth question: Is His words ﴿in which the name of Allah is mentioned much﴾ specific to the mosques, or does it refer to all of them? The answer: Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: It refers to all of them, because Allah, the Exalted, is mentioned much in these places. The more likely view is that it is specific to the mosques, in honor of them, since the remembrance of Allah takes place in them abundantly.

* * *

The sixth question: Why did He mention the monasteries and the churches before the mosques? The answer: Because they are older in existence. It was also said: He placed them later in the mention, as in His words: ﴿And among them is one who is foremost in good deeds by permission of Allah﴾ [Fatir: 32]. And because the first of thought is the last of action. So when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was the best of the messengers and his community the best of communities, they were necessarily the last of them. For this reason he, peace be upon him, said: "We are the last (to come), yet the foremost (in the Hereafter)."

* * *

As for His words, the Exalted, ﴿And Allah will surely help those who help Him﴾, some said: "Those who help Him" means those who accept jihad with acceptance, supporting the religion of Allah, the Exalted. Others said: Rather, what is meant is those who uphold all of His religion. They said this because the help of Allah in the true sense is not valid; what is meant by the help of Allah is the help of His religion, just as it is said of guardianship (wilayah) of Allah and enmity toward Him, similarly. And in His words, ﴿And Allah will surely help those who help Him﴾ is a promise of victory for those who are in this state. The help of Allah, the Exalted, to the servant is that He strengthens him against his enemies until he becomes the victorious one, and that he stands in clarifying the proofs and evidences, and that He assists him in attaining knowledge and acts of obedience. In it there is encouragement toward jihad, since He promised them victory. Then the Exalted explained that He is capable of this victory which He promised to the believers, and that He cannot be prevented from it; and this is the meaning of His words: ﴿Mighty﴾, because the Mighty is the one who cannot be wronged and cannot be prevented from what He wills.

Then, the Glorified and Exalted described those who were given permission to fight in the first verse, saying: ﴿Those who, if We give them authority in the land﴾. What is meant by this authority is sovereignty and the enforceability of command over creation, because what comes first to understanding from His words ﴿if We give them authority in the land﴾ is nothing other than this. Also, if we took it to mean the basic capability, then every servant would be in that state, and then the ordering of the four matters mentioned as the consequence of this would be invalid, because not everyone who is capable of an act performs these things. Having established this, we say: What is meant by them is the emigrants, because His words ﴿those who, if We give them authority﴾ are a description of those mentioned earlier, namely His words ﴿those who have been expelled from their homes﴾, and the Helpers (anṣār) were not expelled from their homes. So the meaning of the verse becomes that Allah, the Exalted, described the emigrants as: if He gives them authority in the land and grants them sovereignty, then they perform the four matters, namely establishing prayer, giving zakat, enjoining what is right, and forbidding what is wrong. But it is established that Allah, the Exalted, gave authority in the land to the four caliphs and granted them sovereignty over it, so it is necessary that they performed these four matters. And since they were enjoining every right and forbidding every wrong, it is necessary that they were upon the truth. Therefore, from this aspect the verse indicates the imamate of the four. It is not permissible to apply the verse to ʿAlī alone, peace be upon him, because the verse is indicative of plurality. And His words ﴿And to Allah belongs the outcome of all matters﴾ indicate that what was mentioned earlier of their sovereignty and dominion is certain to occur. Then, the matters return to Allah, the Exalted, in the end, for He, the Glorified, is the one whose dominion never ceases, and this also confirms what we have said.

[p. 37]

[Page 38]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if they deny you, then the people of Noah, ʿAd, and Thamud had denied [their messengers] before them﴾ ﴿and the people of Abraham and the people of Lot﴾ ﴿and the companions of Madyan. And Moses was denied, so I gave respite to the disbelievers, then I seized them. Then how was My rejection?﴾ ﴿How many a town have We destroyed while it was wrongdoing, so it lies in ruins over its roofs, and [how many] a well abandoned and a lofty palace﴾ ﴿Have they not traveled in the earth so that they would have hearts by which they understand, or ears by which they hear? For indeed it is not the eyes that are blinded, but blinded are the hearts which are within the breasts.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had explained in what preceded the expulsion of the disbelievers of the believers from their homes without right, and permitted fighting against them, and guaranteed the Messenger and the believers victory, and explained that to God belongs the outcome of affairs, He followed it with what serves as consolation to the Messenger (ﷺ) in patience toward what they inflict upon him and upon the believers by way of denial and other things. So He said: "And if they deny you, then all the nations before them denied their prophets," and God mentioned seven of them. If it is asked: "Why did He say: ﴿And Moses was denied﴾ and did not say: 'the people of Moses'?" The answer is in two respects:

The first: Moses, peace be upon him, was not denied by his own people, the Children of Israel; rather, he was denied by others than his people, namely the al-Qibt (the Copts).

The second: It is as if it were said: after mentioning that every people denied its messenger, Moses was also denied, despite the clarity of his signs and the greatness of his miracles. So what do you think about others?

As for His saying: ﴿So I gave respite to the disbelievers﴾, meaning: I granted them respite until the time known to Me, then I seized them with punishment. ﴿Then how was My rejection?﴾ is an interrogative of affirmation (taqrir), meaning: how was My rejection of them through punishment? Was it not certainly realized? Did I not replace their blessing with calamity, their abundance with scarcity, their life with death, and their prosperity with ruin? Did I not give the prophets everything I had promised them of victory over their enemies and of establishing them in the earth? Therefore, O Muhammad, your practice should be patience with them, for indeed He, exalted is He, only delays for a wisdom, so acceptance and submission are necessary, even if that is hard on the heart. Know that without this, consolation is attained by one whose state is below the state of the Messenger, peace be upon him; how then with this, given his rank? Yet at every moment there reaches him from them what increases his grief, so God established His practice of making him patient, state after state. The mention of these deniers has already preceded, and by what kind of punishment of total annihilation (ʿadhab al-istiʾsal) they were destroyed.

Here there is an inquiry: this verse indicates that He, glory be to Him, does to him and to his people everything He did to them and their peoples, except the punishment of total annihilation, for He does not inflict it on the people of Muhammad (ﷺ), even though He has empowered them to kill their enemies and made them firm. Al-Hasan said: The reason for the delay of the punishment of total annihilation with regard to this community is that this punishment is conditioned on two matters. The first: that with God there is a limit of disbelief, so whoever reaches it, He punishes, and whoever does not reach it, He does not punish. The second: that God does not punish a people until He knows that none of them will believe. When both conditions are met, namely that they reach that limit of disbelief and God knows that none of them will believe, then He commands the prophets, and they invoke against their nations, and God answers their supplication and punishes them with the punishment of total annihilation. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿until when the messengers despaired﴾ [Yusuf: 110], that is, of the people's response, and His saying to Noah: ﴿that none will believe of your people except those who have already believed﴾ [Hud: 36]. When God, exalted is He, punishes them, He saves the believers, by His saying: ﴿So when Our command came﴾ [Hud: 82], meaning: with the punishment, We saved Hud. Know that the discussion of this matter has already preceded, so there is no benefit in repeating it. If it is asked: How can the destruction that He sends upon the disbelievers by immediate punishment be described as a "nakir" (a rejection)? We say: when it serves as a deterrent to others and a barrier that turns them away from the like of what necessitated it, it becomes a nakir.

As for His saying ﴿How many a town We have destroyed﴾, there are several issues:

**First issue:** Some have said that the meaning of His saying ﴿fa-ka'ayyin﴾ (how many) is "how many" in the sense of multiplicity, and it has also been said that its meaning is "many a" (rubba). The first is preferable, because it is more emphatic in admonition. It is as though, when He, exalted is He, described the condition of a people among the deniers and that He hastened their destruction, He followed it with something that indicates that there are similar cases, even though they were not mentioned in detail.

**Second issue:** Ibn Kathir, and the people of Kufa and Medina, recited ﴿ahlaknaha﴾ (We have destroyed it) with the nun. Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub recited ﴿ahlaktuha﴾ (I have destroyed it) with the ta'. This is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd, because of His saying in the previous verse ﴿Then I gave the disbelievers respite, then I seized them﴾.

**Third issue:** His saying ﴿ahlaknaha﴾ means "We destroyed its people." His saying "while it is wrongdoing" indicates this, as we have mentioned. It is also possible that the intended meaning is the destruction of the town itself, so that the destruction of its inhabitants is included in its destruction, because when the descending punishment reaches the point of destroying the town, so that it becomes demolished, the destruction of those in it is achieved along with its destruction. However, the first is closer.

As for His saying ﴿while it is wrongdoing, and it is fallen upon its roofs (khawiyatun 'ala 'urushiha)﴾, there are two questions:

**The first question:** What is the meaning of this expression? The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: Every elevated thing that shades you from the roof of a house, a tent, or a canopy is an 'arsh (roof/frame). Al-khawi is the fallen, from khawa al-najm (the star fell) when it sets, or the empty, from khawa al-manzil (the dwelling became empty) when it was emptied of its people. If we interpret khawi as "fallen," the meaning is that it has fallen upon its roofs, that is, its roofs have collapsed to the ground, and then its walls have crumbled and fallen on top of the roofs. If we interpret it as "empty," the meaning is that it is empty of people while its roofs remain intact and whole. He said: It is possible that this is a predicate following a predicate, as if it were said: "it is empty, and it is upon its roofs," meaning that the roofs fell to the ground and came to rest within the walls, while the walls remained standing, so they overlook the fallen roofs. In sum, the verse indicates that they remained a place for taking lesson.

**The second question:** What is the grammatical position (i'rab) of these two clauses, namely ﴿while it is wrongdoing, and so it is fallen upon its roofs﴾? The answer: The first is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal). The second has no position of its own, because it is coordinated with ﴿ahlaknaha﴾, and this verb has no grammatical position. Abu Muslim said: The meaning is "how many a town We have destroyed, while it had been wrongdoing, and now it is fallen."

As for His saying ﴿and an abandoned well and a lofty palace﴾, there are several issues:

**First issue:** Al-Hasan recited ﴿mu'attalatin﴾ from a'talahu, with the same meaning as mu'attalatin. The meaning of "abandoned" is that the well was still full of water and it was possible to draw from it, but it was made idle, that is, left unused, because its people had perished. As for mashid (lofty), there are two views: One is that it means plastered, because gypsum in Medina is called shid. The other is that it means raised and elevated. The meaning is that He, exalted is He, made clear that the town, despite the strain of their building it and their pride in it, was rendered (a place of destruction) because of their disbelief in this description. Likewise the well they had labored over, which became their water source, became abandoned with no drinker or comer to it. The palace they had built firmly with gypsum and made high became conspicuous and empty, with no resident. He, exalted is He, made this a lesson for whoever takes heed and reflects. There is in this an indication that the interpretation of ʿala (upon) as ma'a (with) is preferable, because the implied meaning is "it is empty along with its roofs," and it is known that when it is in that state it is more fitting for taking lesson. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed you pass by them in the morning﴾ [al-Saffat: 137]. And Allah knows best what is correct.

**Second issue:** Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, narrated that Salih descended upon this well together with four thousand people who had believed in him, and Allah, exalted is He, saved them from the punishment, and they were in Hadramawt. It was named so because Salih, when he arrived there, died there. There is a town near the well called Hadur(a), which the people of Salih built. They appointed over it Hasir ibn Julas and made his vizier Sinharib. They remained there for a time, then they disbelieved and worshipped an idol. Allah, exalted is He, sent to them Hanzala ibn Safwan, and they killed him in the marketplace, so Allah, exalted is He, destroyed them, made their well idle, and ruined their palaces. Imam Abu al-Qasim al-Ansari said: This is strange, for I visited the grave of Salih in al-Sham, in a town called 'Akka, so how can it be said that he was in Hadramawt?

As for His saying, ﴿Have they not travelled through the land, so that they would have hearts with which to understand, or ears with which to hear?﴾, its purpose is to mention what completes that consideration (i'tibar, reflection on lessons). Seeing has a great share in consideration, and hearing reports also has a role in it. But these two matters are not complete except through the heart's contemplation (tadabbur), because whoever sees and hears, then does not contemplate or take a lesson, gains nothing at all. If he reflected on what he heard, he would benefit. Therefore He said: ﴿For indeed it is not the eyes that grow blind, but it is the hearts within the breasts that grow blind.﴾ It is as if He said: there is no blindness in their eyes, for they see with them, but the blindness is in their hearts, since they did not benefit from what they saw. Here there are several questions.

The first question: does His saying ﴿Have they not travelled through the land﴾ indicate a command to travel? The answer: it is possible that they had not travelled, so He urged them to travel in order to see the places where those whom God destroyed for their disbelief fell, and to witness their traces, so that they would take a lesson. It is also possible that they had travelled and seen that, but had not taken a lesson, so they were treated as if they had not travelled and had not seen.

The second question: what is the meaning of the pronoun in His saying ﴿For indeed it is not the eyes that grow blind﴾? The answer: this pronoun is the pronoun of the matter and affair (ḍamīr al-qiṣṣa wa al-sha'n). It may be feminine or masculine. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is "fa-innahu" (with the masculine pronoun). It may also be an ambiguous pronoun (ḍamīr mubham) explained by the following word "al-abṣār" (the eyes).

The third question: what is the benefit of mentioning "the breasts" (al-ṣudūr), since everyone knows that the heart is only in the chest? The answer: it is customary that blindness is located in the pupil (al-ḥadaqa). So when it is intended to attribute blindness to the heart, contrary to what is customary, more explanation is needed. As you say: "The sharpness (maḍā') is not for the sword, but for your tongue which is between your jaws." Your saying "which is between your jaws" confirms and establishes what you claimed for the tongue, because the locus of sharpness is that alone and nothing else. It is as if you said: I did not deny sharpness from the sword and affirm it for your tongue by mistake, but I intended it with certainty. In my view there is another aspect to this: the heart may be used as a metaphor (kināya) for thought and contemplation, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart﴾ [Qaf: 37]. Some people hold that the locus of thinking is the brain, so God made clear that its locus is the breast.

The fourth question: does the verse indicate that intellect ('aql) is knowledge ('ilm), and that the locus of knowledge is the heart? The answer: yes, because the intended meaning of His saying ﴿hearts with which they understand﴾ is knowledge. His saying ﴿with which they understand﴾ is like an indication that the heart is the instrument of this understanding (ta'aqqul). Therefore it is necessary to make the heart the locus of understanding. Ignorance is called blindness, because the ignorant person, being bewildered, resembles the blind man.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 22, verse 47–49:

Page 41

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they ask you to hasten the punishment, but Allah will not fail His promise. Indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count.﴾ ﴿And how many a city did I give respite while it was wrongdoing, then I seized it, and to Me is the (final) return.﴾ ﴿Say, "O mankind, I am only to you a clear warner."﴾

Know that when He, the Exalted, related the extent of their denial, that they mocked by asking for the punishment to be hastened, He said: ﴿And they ask you to hasten the punishment﴾. In this is an indication that he, peace be upon him, used to warn them of the punishment if they persisted in their disbelief. Also, their saying: ﴿Why do you not bring us the angels?﴾ [al-Hijr: 7] points to this. So He said: ﴿But Allah will not fail His promise﴾, because the promise of punishment, when it is in the Hereafter rather than in this world, then hastening it would be like a violation of the promise. Then He explained that the intelligent person should not seek to hasten the punishment of the Hereafter, so He said: ﴿Indeed, a day with your Lord﴾, meaning in terms of the punishment that befalls them and its severity, ﴿is like a thousand years﴾ if they remained and were punished, in the multiplicity and severity of the pains. Thus He, glorified is He, made clear that if they knew the state of the punishment of the Hereafter and that it has this description, they would not have sought to hasten it. This is the saying of Abu Muslim, and it is the most preferable of the views.

The second view: the intended meaning is the lengthening of the days of the Hereafter in reckoning, and its meaning returns to something close to what preceded. That is because short days, when they pass in hardship, become prolonged. So how would prolonged days be when they pass in hardship? Moreover, a punishment whose days are lengthened to this degree is not something the intelligent person should seek to hasten.

The third view: one day and a thousand years are equal in relation to Him, because He is the All-Powerful, whom nothing can frustrate. So if they do not find it strange that a day is granted respite, then they should not find it strange either that a thousand years is granted respite.

As for His saying: ﴿And how many a city did I give respite while it was wrongdoing﴾, the meaning is: how many a city did I delay their destruction while they persisted in their wrongdoing, so they were deceived by that delay; then I seized them by sending down the punishment upon them. Along with that, their punishment is stored up for when they return to Me, and this is the explanation of His saying: ﴿and to Me is the (final) return﴾. If it is asked: why did He say earlier: ﴿So how many a city did We destroy while it was wrongdoing﴾ with "fa" (then), while here He says: ﴿And how many a city did I give respite﴾ with "wa" (and)? We say: the first came in place of His saying: ﴿So how was My denunciation?﴾. As for this, its ruling is the ruling of the two sentences preceding it that are conjoined with "wa", namely His saying: ﴿Allah will not fail His promise, and indeed a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count﴾.

As for His saying: ﴿Say, "O mankind, I am only to you a clear warner"﴾, the meaning is that He, may He be exalted, commanded His Messenger to continue to frighten and warn them, and that what they say of hastening the punishment in mockery should not prevent him from continuing the warning, and that he should say to them: I was only sent as a warner, so your mockery of that does not stop me from it.

[p. 42]

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds, for them is forgiveness and a generous provision.﴾ ﴿And those who strive against Our signs, seeking to frustrate them, they are the companions of the Blazing Fire.﴾

Know that when the Exalted made clear to the Messenger (ﷺ) that he must say to them, "I am only a plain warner," He followed this by commanding him to give them good tidings and warning, because a man is only a warner when he mentions the promise to the obedient and the threat to the disobedient. So He said: ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾, combining the two descriptions. This is evidence that righteous deeds lie outside the name of faith (īmān), and by it the view of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school) is refuted. Faith includes everything obligatory of belief in the heart and affirmation by the tongue, and righteous deeds include the performance of every obligation and the abandonment of every prohibited act. Then the Glorified showed that whoever combines the two, God the Exalted combines for him forgiveness and generous provision.

As for forgiveness, it may refer either to the forgiveness of minor sins (ṣaghā'ir), or to the forgiveness of major sins (kabā'ir) after repentance, or to their forgiveness before repentance. The first two are obligatory according to the opponent, and the performance of an obligation is not called forgiveness. So the third remains: it indicates pardon for the people of major sins among the people of the qibla (ahl al-qibla, i.e., the Muslims). As for generous provision, it is an indication of reward. Its generosity may be taken to refer to negative attributes, namely that the person there is free from needing to earn, from enduring hardships and humiliation in earning, from committing sins and baseness on account of it. It may also refer to positive attributes, namely that it is abundant provision, lasting, pure of any harm, and accompanied by honour and reverence. It is better to take "generous" as indicating all of these attributes. This explains the state of the believers.

As for the state of the disbelievers, He said: ﴿And those who strive against Our signs, seeking to frustrate them﴾. The meaning is that they exerted themselves in rejecting them and denying them, when they called them sorcery, poetry, and "tales of the ancients". It is said of one who exerts his utmost effort in a matter that "he strove (sa'ā) in it", by way of extension, since he reached the limit in exerting effort, just as when a walker reaches the limit of his strength, it is said of him that he "strove." He mentioned the signs but meant denying them, metaphorically. The author of the Kashshāf (al-Zamakhsharī's commentary) said: It is said "sa'ā fī amr fulān" when one sets it right or corrupts it by his striving. As for mu'ājizīn, it is said: "'ājaztuhu", meaning I hoped to frustrate him.

They differed about the intended meaning: are they frustrating God, or the Messenger and the believers? The closer view is the second, because if they deny God, it is impossible for them to hope to frustrate Him, and if they affirm Him, it is far-fetched that they would believe they could render Him powerless and overcome Him. But it is possible for them to think this regarding the Messenger, through tricks and schemes.

As for those who said that the meaning is frustrating God, they gave several explanations:
First: the meaning of "frustrating" is overcoming and escaping their Lord from His punishment and reckoning, since they denied the Resurrection. Second: they hinder others from believing in God and discourage them through encouragement and intimidation. Third: they frustrate God by introducing doubts into people's hearts.

The answer to the first: whoever denies the very existence of a thing is not described as overcoming the one who does that thing. And whoever interprets the verse in this way must mean that they thought they could overcome the Messenger (ﷺ) regarding what he said about the gathering and the raising of the dead. The answer to the second and third: overcoming, in reality, returns to the Messenger and the community, not to God the Exalted.

As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿They are the companions of the Blazing Fire﴾, the meaning is that they will abide in it, and He likened them, in respect of permanence, to the companion (ṣāḥib). If it is said: He (peace be upon him) in this verse gave good news to the believers first and warned the disbelievers second, so the analogical form would have been: "Say, O people, I am only a bearer of good news and a warner to you." We say: the discourse is directed at the polytheists, and "O people" is an address to them, and they are those of whom it was said: ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth?﴾ [Ghāfir 40:82], and they were described as hasty. The mention of the believers and their reward was placed in between only to increase their rage and their harm.

[Page 44]

Its wording: ﴿Never did We send before you any messenger or prophet but that when he wished, Satan cast into his wish. But God abrogates what Satan casts, then God makes His verses firm. God is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾ ﴿That He may make what Satan casts a trial for those in whose hearts is a sickness and whose hearts are hardened. Indeed, the wrongdoers are in extreme opposition.﴾ ﴿And that those given knowledge may know that it is the truth from your Lord, so they believe in it and their hearts humble before Him. Indeed, God guides those who believe to a straight path.﴾ ﴿And those who disbelieve will not cease to be in doubt about it until the Hour comes upon them suddenly, or there comes to them the punishment of a barren day.﴾ ﴿Sovereignty on that Day belongs to God; He will judge between them. Those who believed and did righteous deeds will be in Gardens of Bliss.﴾ ﴿But those who disbelieved and denied Our signs, for them will be a humiliating punishment.﴾

As for His saying, ﴿Never did We send before you any messenger or prophet but that when he wished, Satan cast into his wish﴾, there are several issues concerning it.

The first issue: Some people said: The messenger (rasul, one sent with a message) is the one who was told (by revelation) and sent, while the prophet (nabi) is the one who was not sent, but was inspired or saw (visions) in sleep. Others said: Every messenger is a prophet, but not every prophet is a messenger; this is the view of al-Kalbi and al-Farra'. The Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school) said: Every messenger is a prophet and every prophet is a messenger, and there is no difference between them. They argued against the first view with several points:

One: This verse indicates that a prophet may be sent, and likewise His saying, ﴿We never sent a prophet to a town…﴾ [Al-A'raf: 94]. Two: God addressed Muhammad sometimes as "prophet" and sometimes as "messenger," which shows there is no contradiction between the two designations, whereas according to the first view there would be a contradiction. Three: He explicitly stated that he is the Seal of the Prophets. Four: The derivation of the word nabi is either from naba' (news), meaning information, or from their saying nabaa, meaning he was elevated, and both meanings are only realized by accepting the message.

As for the second view, know that none of those points refutes it; rather, this verse indicates it, because He conjoined "prophet" to "messenger," and that requires distinction; it is the case of the general conjoined to the specific. He also said elsewhere: ﴿How many prophets did We send among the earlier peoples?﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 6], which shows that he was a prophet, then God made him a messenger. This accords with our statement that there is a report: It was said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): How many messengers were there? He said: Three hundred and thirteen. It was said: And how many prophets? He said: One hundred and twenty-four thousand, a great multitude.

Once this is established, we say: They mentioned several differences between the messenger and the prophet:

One: A messenger among the prophets is the one who, along with a miracle, was given a book revealed to him, whereas a prophet who is not a messenger is one to whom no book was revealed, and who was only commanded to call to the book of one before him.

Two: Whoever possesses a miracle, possesses a book, and abrogates the law of one before him is a messenger; whoever does not combine these qualities is a prophet and not a messenger. These (Mu'tazilah) are obliged to not count Isaac, Jacob, Job, Jonah, Aaron, David and Solomon as messengers, because they did not bring an abrogating book.

Three: Whoever was visited by an angel openly and commanded to call the people is a messenger; whoever is not like this, but saw in sleep that he was a messenger, or was told by one of the messengers that he is a messenger of God, is a prophet who is not a messenger. This is the preferable view.

* * *

The second issue: The commentators mentioned, regarding the cause of revelation of this verse, that "when the Messenger (ﷺ) saw his people turning away from him, and it grieved him what he saw of their distancing themselves from what he had brought them, he wished in himself that something from God would come to him that would bring him closer to his people. This was out of his eagerness for their faith. One day he sat in a gathering of the Quraysh assemblies, with many people in it, and he wished on that day that nothing from God would come that would make them flee from him, and he wished for that. So God revealed the surah ﴿By the star when it sets﴾ [An-Najm: 1]. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited it until he reached His saying: ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-Uzza, and Manat, the third, the other?﴾ [An-Najm: 19–20]. Satan cast upon his tongue: ‘Those are the exalted cranes, whose intercession is hoped for.’ When the Quraysh heard that, they rejoiced, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) continued his recitation until he recited the whole surah, then he prostrated, and the Muslims prostrated because of his prostration, and all those in the mosque of the polytheists prostrated as well, so no believer or disbeliever remained in the mosque without prostrating, except al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah and Abu Uhayhah Sa'id ibn al-As. They took a handful of dust from the valley and raised it to their foreheads and prostrated upon it, because they were two elderly men who could not prostrate. The Quraysh dispersed, pleased with what they had heard, and said: Muhammad has mentioned our gods with the best mention. When evening came upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ), Jibril (Gabriel) came to him and said: What have you done? You recited to the people what I did not bring you from God, and you said what I did not say to you! So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) grieved greatly and feared God with a great fear, until there was revealed His saying: ﴿Never did We send before you any messenger or prophet but that when he wished, Satan cast into his wish…﴾ [Al-Hajj: 52]."

This is the narration of the general exegetes (al-mufassirun al-zahiriyyun, those who take the apparent sense). As for the scholars of verification (ahl al-tahqiq), they said: This narration is false and fabricated, and they argued for this from the Qur'an, the Sunnah, and reason.

As for the Qur'an, there are several points:

One: His saying: ﴿Had he fabricated against Us some sayings, We would have seized him by the right hand, then We would have cut from him the aorta﴾ [Al-Haqqah: 44–46].

Two: His saying: ﴿Say: It is not for me to change it on my own accord; I follow only what is revealed to me﴾ [Yunus: 15].

Three: His saying: ﴿Nor does he speak from desire. It is only revelation that is revealed﴾ [An-Najm: 3–4]. So if he had recited after this verse, "Those are the exalted cranes," then the falsehood of God would have been manifest immediately, and no Muslim would say that.

Four: His saying: ﴿And indeed they almost tempted you away from what We revealed to you, to fabricate other than it against Us; and then they would have taken you as a friend﴾ [Al-Isra': 73]. The word "almost" (kada) according to some means: the matter came close to being so, but it did not happen.

Five: His saying: ﴿And if We had not made you firm, you would have almost inclined toward them a little﴾ [Al-Isra': 74]. The word "law-la" (if not) indicates the non-occurrence of one thing due to the non-occurrence of another, which shows that this slight inclination did not take place.

Six: His saying: ﴿Thus, that We may strengthen your heart thereby﴾ [Al-Furqan: 32].

Seven: His saying: ﴿We will make you recite, and you will not forget﴾ [Al-A'la: 6].

As for the Sunnah, it is what is reported from Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Khuzaymah, that he was asked about this story and said: This is a fabrication of the heretics (zanadiqah), and he wrote a book on it. Imam Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn al-Husayn al-Bayhaqi said: This story is not established in terms of transmission. He then began discussing that the narrators of this story are impugned. Also, al-Bukhari reported in his Sahih that "the Prophet, peace be upon him, recited Surah al-Najm and the Muslims, the polytheists, humans and jinn prostrated in it," and there is nothing in it about the story of the cranes. This hadith has been reported through many routes, and none of them at all contains the story of the cranes.

As for reason, there are several points:

One: Whoever permits for the Messenger (ﷺ) the glorification of idols has disbelieved, because it is known by necessity that the greatest of his striving was in negating idols.

Two: At the beginning he (ﷺ) could not pray and recite the Qur'an at the Ka'bah safe from the harm of the polytheists, who at times would stretch their hands toward him. He would only pray when they were not present, at night or in times of solitude, and this invalidates their claim.

Three: Their hostility toward the Messenger was too great for them to acknowledge this degree of recitation without first ascertaining the reality of the matter. How then did they all agree that he glorified their gods, to the point that they fell down prostrating, when he had not shown them agreement with them?

Four: His saying: ﴿So God abrogates what Satan casts, then God makes His verses firm﴾. The making firm of the verses by removing what Satan casts upon the Messenger is stronger than abrogating them with these verses in which doubt remains. So if God wills to make the verses firm lest what is not Qur'an be mixed with the Qur'an, then that Satan be prevented from this altogether is more fitting.

Five, which is the strongest of the points: If we permitted that, the security of His law would be lifted, and we would permit that each of the rulings and laws could be like that, and His saying would be invalidated: ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord; and if you do not, then you have not conveyed His message; and God will protect you from the people﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 67]. For in reason there is no difference between a deficiency in revelation and an addition to it.

By these points we know, in general terms, that this story is fabricated. At most, a group of commentators mentioned it, but they did not reach the level of mass transmission (tawatur), and a single report (khabar al-wahid) does not oppose the textual and rational proofs that are mass-transmitted.

Now let us begin the detailed discussion. We say: The word tamanni (wishing) comes in the language with two meanings: One: the wishing of the heart. Two: recitation. God said: ﴿Among them are unlettered ones who do not know the Book except as wishes (amani)﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 78], meaning except as recitation, because the unlettered one does not know the Qur'an from the written copy, but knows it only by recitation. Hassan said:

"He wished for the Book of God at the first night and its last, and met the death-decree of the fates."

It was said: Recitation was only called "wish" (umniyyah) because the reciter, when he reaches a verse of mercy, wishes to attain it, and when he reaches a verse of punishment, wishes not to be afflicted by it. Abu Muslim said: Tamanni means taqdir (determining, decreeing), and tamanna is a form of tafa''ala from muniytu, and al-maniyyah is a person's death at the time God has decreed; and "manaa Allah laka" means God decreed for you. The transmitters of the language said: al-umniyyah means recitation, and they argued with Hassan's verse; this returns to the root we have mentioned, for the reciter determines the letters and mentions them one by one. The summary of this discussion is that al-umniyyah is either recitation or a passing thought.

If we interpret it as recitation, there are two views. The first: God intended by it what the Messenger (ﷺ) might err in, and what might be confused for the reciter, not what they narrated from his saying, "Those are the exalted cranes." The second: The intended meaning is the occurrence of this phrase in his recitation. Then those who hold this view differed in several ways:

The first way: The Prophet (ﷺ) did not say "Those are the exalted cranes," nor did Satan say it, nor did anyone say it. Rather, when he (peace be upon him) recited Surah al-Najm, the matter became confused for the disbelievers, so they supposed that some of his words were what they narrated as their saying, "Those are the exalted cranes," and this is in accordance with the custom of mistaking some words for something other than what is being said. This view was held by a group, and it is weak for several reasons.

[p. 46]

The first point: such a delusion can only occur regarding something that people are accustomed to hearing. As for what has not been heard, such a delusion does not arise concerning it. Second: even if it were so, this delusion would have affected some of the listeners and not others, since custom prevents a large crowd from all agreeing, at the same moment, on one false imagining about things perceived by the senses. Third: if it were so, it would not be attributed to Satan.

The second aspect: They said that this utterance was the speech of a Satan of the jinn. This would be by uttering words of his own accord, inserting them during some pauses of that recitation so that they would be taken to be of the same kind as what was heard from the Messenger (ﷺ). They said: What confirms this is that there is no disagreement that the jinn and the devils speak, so there is nothing to prevent Satan from producing a voice like the voice of the Messenger, peace be upon him, and speaking these words in the midst of the Messenger's speech, during his silence. When those present heard that word in a voice like the Messenger's, and did not see another person, they supposed that it was the speech of the Messenger. Then this would not be damaging to prophethood, since it was not his action. This also is weak. For if you allow that Satan could speak in the midst of the speech of the Messenger (ﷺ) with words that would appear to all listeners to be the speech of the Messenger, this possibility would remain in everything the Messenger says, and it would lead to the removal of trust in the entire Shari'ah. If it is said: This possibility exists in everything, but if it had occurred, it would have been necessary, in the wisdom of God the Exalted, that the situation be explained, as in this incident, to remove the confusion. We reply: It is not obligatory upon God to remove all possibilities, as in the case of the ambiguous (mutashabihat) matters. And since it is not obligatory upon God to do that, the possibility is open for everything.

The third aspect: It is said that the one who spoke this was some of the devils of mankind, namely the disbelievers. When the Messenger (ﷺ) reached this place in the recitation of this surah and mentioned the names of their gods, and they knew from his habit that he would disparage them, one of those present said "tilka al-gharaniq al-ula" (those are the exalted cranes), and the matter became confused for the people because of the great noise and the loud clamor, and their seeking to refute him and to drown out his recitation. Perhaps this happened during his prayer, because they would come close to him during his prayer, listen to his recitation, and make noise during it. It was also said that when he (peace be upon him) recited the Qur'an to the Quraysh, he would pause between the verses, and one of those present threw that utterance into those pauses, so the people imagined it was part of the recitation of the Messenger (ﷺ). Then God the Exalted attributed that to Satan, because it comes about first through his whisperings, and because He (glory be to Him) made that speaker a Satan in himself. This also is weak, for two reasons:

The first: If it were so, it would have been obligatory upon the Messenger (ﷺ) to remove the doubt, to state the truth clearly, to rebuke that speaker, and to make known that this word had come from someone other than him.

The second: If he had done that, it would have been more worthy of being transmitted. If it is said: The Messenger (ﷺ) did not do that because he had already conveyed the surah in its entirety to the community without this addition, so this did not lead to confusion, just as his forgetfulness in prayer does not lead to confusion after he has finished it. We reply: The Qur'an was not fixed in one state during his lifetime, for verses would come to him and he would add them to their surahs. So conveying that surah without this addition was not a cause for removing the confusion. Moreover, if it were so, he would not have deserved the reproach from God the Exalted that the people have related.

The fourth aspect: The one who uttered this was the Messenger (ﷺ) himself. This has three possibilities: he said this word either through forgetfulness, or by compulsion, or by choice.

As for the first possibility, that he (peace be upon him) said this word through forgetfulness: as is related from Qatadah and Muqatil, they both said: He (peace be upon him) was praying near the Maqam, he dozed, and these two phrases slipped from his tongue. When he finished the surah, he prostrated, and everyone in the mosque prostrated. The polytheists rejoiced at what they had heard. Then Gabriel (peace be upon him) came to him and asked him to recite it, and when he reached "the exalted cranes" he said: "I did not bring you this." So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) grieved until this verse was revealed. This also is weak, for several reasons:

First: If this forgetfulness were permissible, it would be permissible in all other places, and in that case trust in the Shari'ah would disappear.

Second: The one who is forgetful cannot produce words like these, which conform to the meter of the surah, its manner, and its meaning. For we know by necessity that if someone were to recite a poem, it would not be possible for him to forget so that a line of poetry in its meter, meaning, and style occurs from him.

Third: Suppose he had spoken those words through forgetfulness. How was he not alerted to them when he recited them to Gabriel (peace be upon him)? This is evident.

As for the second possibility, that he (peace be upon him) spoke those words by compulsion, which is what some people said: that Satan forced the Prophet (ﷺ)

[p. 47]

to say these words. This too is invalid, for several reasons:
