Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 22, verses 77–78 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, bow down, prostrate yourselves, worship your Lord, and do good, that perhaps you may prosper.﴾ ﴿And strive for Allah with the striving due to Him. He has chosen you and has not placed upon you in religion any hardship, the religion of your father Ibrahim. He named you "Muslims" before, and in this [Revelation], so that the Messenger may be a witness over you and you may be witnesses over mankind. So establish prayer, give zakah, and hold fast to Allah. He is your Protector, and what an excellent Protector and what an excellent Helper.﴾

Know that when He, glorified is He, had spoken about the divine matters and then about prophethood, He followed this with speech on the sharia (divine law), and it is in four aspects:
The first of them: specifying the one commanded.
The second: the categories of what is commanded.
The third: mention of what makes these commands binding to accept.
The fourth: affirming that obligation.

As for the first type, which is specifying the one commanded, it is His saying: ﴿O you who believe﴾. There are two views concerning it. One: it means all who are legally responsible, whether believer or disbeliever, because the obligation of these things is general to all who are legally responsible, so there is no sense in restricting it to believers. The second: that what is meant is the believers only. As for the first, the wording is explicit about it; as for the second, His saying after that: ﴿He has chosen you﴾, His saying: ﴿He named you Muslims﴾, and His saying: ﴿that you may be witnesses over mankind﴾, all of this fits only believers. The most that can be said is: if this is obligatory for everyone, what is the benefit of restricting it to believers? We say: singling them out by mention does not imply the negation of it for others; rather, this verse has shown that they, in particular, are commanded with these things, and other verses have shown that all are commanded with them. It may also be said: the benefit of the specification is that when the general address came again and again, and then only the believers accepted it, Allah singled them out with this address so that it would serve as an encouragement for them to persist in accepting it, and as an honouring of them for that acknowledgment and the specification.

As for the second type, which is the thing commanded, Allah has mentioned four matters.

The first: prayer, which is what is meant by His saying: ﴿bow down and prostrate﴾. This is because the most noble pillars of prayer are bowing and prostration, and prayer is specifically characterised by these two pillars, so mentioning them functions as mentioning prayer. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, reported that at the beginning of their Islam people used to bow but not prostrate, until this verse was revealed.

The second: His saying: ﴿worship your Lord﴾. They have mentioned several interpretations of it:
One: worship Him and do not worship other than Him.
Second: worship your Lord in all that is commanded and forbidden.
Third: perform bowing, prostration and all other acts of obedience in the manner of worship, because it is not enough that an act is done without intending by it the worship of Allah, the Exalted; for it does not benefit regarding reward unless it is intended for the worship of Allah. Therefore He joined this clause after bowing and prostration.

The third: His saying: ﴿and do good﴾. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: by it is meant maintaining family ties and noble character. My view on the ordering in this sequence is that prayer is a kind of worship, and worship is a kind of doing good, because doing good divides into service to the One worshipped, which is an expression of glorifying the command of Allah, and into kindness, which is an expression of compassion towards the creation of Allah, and it includes righteousness, enjoining what is good, charity to the poor, and good speech to people. So it is as if He, glorified is He, said: I have obligated you to prayer; rather, I have obligated you to what is more general than it, which is worship; rather, I have obligated you to what is more general than worship, which is doing good deeds. As for His saying: ﴿that perhaps you may prosper﴾, it has been said that its meaning is: so that you may prosper. Prosperity is attaining the bliss of the Hereafter. Imam Abu al-Qasim al-Ansari said: "perhaps" (la'alla) is a word expressing hope, for a person rarely is free, in performing an obligation, from some shortcoming, and he is not certain that what he has done is accepted by Allah, the Exalted, and the outcomes are also hidden. "And each is made easy for that for which he was created."
* * *
The fourth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And strive for Allah with the striving due to Him﴾. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: ﴿for Allah﴾ means in the essence of Allah and for His sake. It is said: "he is the true scholar and the earnest scholar," meaning, truly a scholar and earnestly so, and from this comes ﴿with the striving due to Him﴾. Here there are questions:

The first question: What is the purpose of this idafa (construct phrase), when the expected wording would be "the due striving in it" or "the due striving of you in it," as He said: ﴿And strive for Allah with the striving due to Him﴾? The answer: the idafa is made with the slightest connection and specification. Since the striving is specific to Allah, in that it is done for His sake and for His purpose, the idafa to Him is valid.

The second question: What is this striving? The answer: there are several views:
One: that what is meant is fighting the disbelievers specifically, and the meaning of ﴿due striving﴾ is that one does nothing except as worship, not out of desire for worldly things, whether reputation or spoils.
The second: that they strive at the end as they strove at the beginning. Their striving at the beginning was stronger, and they were steadier in it, like their conduct on the day of Badr. It has been reported from Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said to Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf: "Do you not know that we used to recite: ﴿And strive for Allah with the striving due to Him﴾ at the end of time, as you strove at its beginning?" Abd al-Rahman said: "And when will that be, O Commander of the Faithful?" He said: "When the Banu Umayyah become the rulers and the Banu al-Mughirah the viziers." Know that it is unlikely that this addition is from the Qur'an, for otherwise it would have been transmitted like its counterparts; and perhaps, if this is authentically from the Messenger, he said it as an explanation of the verse. It is also reported from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he recited: "And strive for Allah with the striving due to Him, as you strove the first time." Umar said: "Who is it that we were commanded to strive for?" He said: "Two tribes of Quraysh, Makhzum and Abd Shams." He said: "You have spoken truly."
The third: Ibn Abbas said: "The due striving: do not fear the blame of any blamer in Allah's cause."
The fourth: al-Dahhak said: "And work for Allah with the work due to Him."
The fifth: exert your utmost effort in reviving the religion of Allah and establishing His rights, by fighting with the hand and the tongue, and all that is possible, and restrain yourselves from desire and inclination.
The sixth: Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak said: "The due striving: the striving against the self and desire."
* * *
When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned from the Battle of Tabuk, he said: "We have returned from the lesser striving to the greater striving." The best view is that this should be understood as applying to all the obligations: everything that one is commanded to do and forbidden from is, in observing it, a form of striving.

The third question: Is what has been transmitted from Muqatil and al-Kalbi correct, that this verse is abrogated (mansukh) by His saying: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [al-Taghabun: 16], just as His saying: ﴿Fear Allah as He should be feared﴾ [Al 'Imran: 102] is abrogated by that? The answer: this is far-fetched, because obligation is conditioned on capacity, by His saying: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286]. How could Allah say "strive for Allah" in a manner you cannot do? And how, when striving at first was so restricted that it was not permissible for one to flee from ten, and then Allah lightened it by His saying: ﴿Now Allah has lightened your burden﴾ [al-Anfal: 66]? Would it be permissible, in that case, for Him to obligate it in a way that cannot be borne, so that it could be said that it is abrogated?

The third type: explaining what makes these commands binding to accept, and it is three things. The first: His saying: ﴿He has chosen you﴾. Its meaning is that obligation is an honour from Allah, exalted is He, to the servant. When He has specified you with this honour, He has specified you with the greatest of honours, and chosen you for His service and occupation with His obedience. What rank is higher than this? And what happiness is above this? It is also possible that in ﴿He has chosen you﴾ it means He has specified you with guidance, assistance and facilitation.
* * *
As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He has not placed upon you in religion any hardship﴾, it is like an answer to an objection that is raised, which is: obligation, although it is an honour that is obligatory, as you have mentioned, is nonetheless difficult and severe upon the self. So Allah, exalted is He, answered it with His saying: ﴿And He has not placed upon you in religion any hardship﴾. It is reported that Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "How can Allah say: ﴿And He has not placed upon you in religion any hardship﴾, when He has forbidden us from fornication and theft?" Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "Yes, but the burden that was upon the Children of Israel has been removed from you." Here there are questions:

The first question: What is hardship (haraj) in the original language? The answer: it is reported from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said to a man from Hudhayl: "What do you count as hardship among you?" He said: "Narrowness." And from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about that, and he said: 'Narrowness.'"

The second question: What is meant by hardship in the verse? The answer: it has been said that it is the provision of concessions. Whoever cannot pray standing should pray sitting, and whoever cannot do that should make gestures; and He permitted the fasting person to break the fast while travelling and to shorten the prayer during travel. Also, He, glorified is He, did not test His servant with any sin without making a way out of it for him, either by repentance or by expiation. And from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both: "Whoever is given a concession and turns away from it will be obligated on the Day of Resurrection to carry the weight of a tinnin until judgment is passed among people." And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "When two matters are gathered, the one more beloved to Allah, the Exalted, is the easier of the two." And from Ka'b: "Allah gave this nation three things that He gave to none but the prophets: He made them witnesses over mankind, He did not place upon them any hardship in religion, and He said: 'Call upon Me, I will respond to you.'"

They said: when Allah created disbelief and disobedience in the disbeliever and the sinner, and then forbade him from them, that would be among the greatest hardship, and that is negated by the clear text of this verse. The answer: when He commanded him to abandon disbelief, and abandoning disbelief requires turning his knowledge into ignorance, then Allah has commanded the responsible person to turn Allah's knowledge into ignorance, and that is among the greatest hardship. But when the two feet stand equal, the question is dissolved.

One of them, which is the view of al-Farra': it is in the accusative by the meaning of what precedes it, as if it were said: "He has broadened your religion with the broadening of the religion of your father Ibrahim," then the governing noun was omitted and the governed noun was put in its place.
The second: that it is in the accusative as praise and glorification, meaning: "I mean by the religion the religion of your father Ibrahim." The Arabs loved Ibrahim, peace be upon him, because they were his descendants, so drawing attention to this served as a means for their becoming receptive to accepting this religion. Here there are questions:

The first question: Why did He say: ﴿the religion of your father Ibrahim﴾ and not include in the address the believers who were in the time of the Messenger (ﷺ) and were not of his offspring? The answer is from two aspects.
One: since most of them were of his offspring, such as the Messenger and his kin and all the Arabs, it was permissible.
The second, which is the view of al-Hasan: Allah made the sanctity of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, upon the Muslims like the sanctity of a father upon his son. From this is His saying: ﴿The Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves﴾ [al-Ahzab: 6], so He made his sanctity like that of a father upon a son, and the sanctity of his wives like that of mothers, as He said: ﴿and his wives are their mothers﴾ [al-Ahzab: 6].

The second question: This requires that the religion of Muhammad be the same as the religion of Abraham, peace be upon them both, so that the Messenger would have no specific sharia of his own. This is reinforced by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then We revealed to you, [O Muhammad], to follow the religion of Abraham﴾ [an-Nahl: 123]. The answer: This statement was addressed to the idol-worshippers. It is as if He, Exalted is He, said: worship of God and abandoning the idols is the religion of Abraham. As for the details of the sharia, they have no connection to this point.

The third question: What is the meaning of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He named you Muslims before [this]﴾? The answer: There are two opinions on this. The first is that the pronoun refers to Abraham, peace be upon him, for every prophet has a granted supplication (da'wah mustajabah). This is the saying of Abraham, peace and blessings be upon him: ﴿Our Lord, make us Muslims [in submission] to You and from our descendants a Muslim nation [in submission] to You﴾ [al-Baqarah: 128]. So God, Exalted is He, answered him and made them the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ). It is also narrated that he, peace and blessings be upon him, informed that God, Exalted is He, would send Muhammad with the like of his religion, and that his nation would be named "the Muslims." The second is that the pronoun refers to God, Exalted is He, in His saying: ﴿He has chosen you﴾. Atta' narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that he said: "God named you Muslims before," i.e., in all the books, "and in this," i.e., in the Qur'an. This interpretation is closer, because He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿that the Messenger may be a witness over you and that you may be witnesses over the people﴾. So He made clear that He named them with this for this purpose, and this befits none but God. It is also supported by the recitation of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "God named you." The meaning is that He, glorified is He, [named you so] in the books that preceded the Qur'an, and in the Qur'an He also made clear your virtue over the nations and named you with this most noble name, for the sake of the testimony mentioned. So just as God has singled you out with this honour, worship Him and do not reject His obligations. This is the third reason (al-'illah al-thalithah) requiring acceptance of the obligation. As for the discussion of how the Messenger can be a witness over us and how his nation can be witnesses over the people, it has preceded in Surat al-Baqarah, and we explained there that from it is derived what indicates that consensus (ijma') is a proof.

The fourth type: explanation of what serves as a confirmation of what has passed, and it is His saying: ﴿So establish prayer and give zakah﴾
Page 66
It must be understood as referring to the obligatory acts, because they are the well-known ones. ﴿And hold fast to God﴾, i.e., to His rational and transmitted proofs, His kindnesses and His protection. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Ask God for protection from all that is forbidden." al-Qaffal said: Make God a safeguard for you against what you fear. ﴿He is your Protector (mawla)﴾, your Master and the one who disposes over you, ﴿so what an excellent Protector and what an excellent Helper﴾. It is as if He, glorified is He, said: I am your Protector, indeed I am your Helper and sufficient for you. Know that the Mu'tazilah argued with these verses in several ways.

The first: His saying: ﴿that you may be witnesses over the people﴾ indicates that He, glorified is He, intended faith from all. For He does not make a witness over His servants except one who is just and approved. So when He wills that you be witnesses over the people, He has willed that you all be righteous and just, and we know that among them are wrongdoers (fussaq). This indicates that God, Exalted is He, willed for the wrongdoer that he be just.

The second: His saying: ﴿and hold fast to God﴾. How is it possible to hold fast to Him when evil exists only from Him?

The third: His saying: ﴿what an excellent Protector﴾. For if it were as the People of the Sunnah say, that He created most of His servants in order to create disbelief and corruption in them and then punish them, He would not be an excellent Protector; rather, there would be no wicked master except that he is better than Him. So He would have to be described as "a wretched Protector," and that is false. This indicates that He, glorified is He, willed for all of them only righteousness. If it is said: Why could it not be that He is an excellent Protector only for the believers, just as He is an excellent Helper only for them? We say: He, Exalted is He, is the Protector of both believers and disbelievers together, so it must be said that He is an excellent Protector for the believers and a wretched Protector for the disbelievers. If they commit this, they have rejected the Qur'an and the consensus and openly insulted God, Exalted is He.

The fourth: His saying: ﴿He named you Muslims before﴾ indicates the establishment of sharia names, and that they come from God, Exalted is He; for if they were linguistic, they would not be attributed to God, Exalted is He, in a specific way.

The answer to the first: God's being willing for it to be the case that He makes [them] witnesses entails that He is willing for them to be just. So we say: If the willing of a thing entails the willing of its necessary consequences, then the willing of faith from the disbeliever necessitates that it entail willing the ignorance of God, Exalted is He, and so it follows that He, Exalted is He, wills the ignorance of Himself. And if that is not necessary, the argument falls.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿and hold fast to God﴾, it is said: this too applies to you, for He, glorified is He, created desire in the heart of the wrongdoer and reinforced it, created the object of desire and brought it near him, removed the obstacle, then gave the devils of mankind and jinn power over him, and He knew that he would inevitably fall into wickedness and error. In the case of the witness, whoever does this would be a wretched protector. So if the analogy of the absent to the witnessed is valid, this is binding upon you; and if it is invalid, your argument falls entirely.

He has chosen you and has not placed upon you in religion any hardship, the religion of your father Ibrahim. He named you "Muslims" before, and in this [Revelation], so that the Messenger may be a witness over you and you may be witnesses over mankind. Know that when He, glorified is He, had spoken about the divine matters and then about prophethood, He followed this with speech on the sharia (divine law), and it is in four aspects:
The first of them: specifying the one commanded.
The second: the categories of what is commanded.
The third: mention of what makes these commands binding to accept.
The fourth: affirming that obligation.

As for the first type, which is specifying the one commanded, it is His saying: ﴿O you who believe﴾. There are two views concerning it. One: it means all who are legally responsible, whether believer or disbeliever, because the obligation of these things is general to all who are legally responsible, so there is no sense in restricting it to believers. We say: singling them out by mention does not imply the negation of it for others; rather, this verse has shown that they, in particular, are commanded with these things, and other verses have shown that all are commanded with them. It may also be said: the benefit of the specification is that when the general address came again and again, and then only the believers accepted it, Allah singled them out with this address so that it would serve as an encouragement for them to persist in accepting it, and as an honouring of them for that acknowledgment and the specification.

From this is His saying: ﴿The Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves﴾ [al-Ahzab: 6], so He made his sanctity like that of a father upon a son, and the sanctity of his wives like that of mothers, as He said: ﴿and his wives are their mothers﴾ [al-Ahzab: 6].

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 22, verse 77–78 (part 2 of 2):

The second question: This requires that the religion of Muhammad be the same as the religion of Abraham, peace be upon them both, so that the Messenger would have no specific sharia of his own. This is reinforced by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then We revealed to you, [O Muhammad], to follow the religion of Abraham﴾ [an-Nahl: 123]. The answer: This statement was addressed to the idol-worshippers. It is as if He, Exalted is He, said: worship of God and abandoning the idols is the religion of Abraham. As for the details of the sharia, they have no connection to this point.

The third question: What is the meaning of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He named you Muslims before [this]﴾? The answer: There are two opinions on this. The first is that the pronoun refers to Abraham, peace be upon him, for every prophet has a granted supplication (da'wah mustajabah). This is the saying of Abraham, peace and blessings be upon him: ﴿Our Lord, make us Muslims [in submission] to You and from our descendants a Muslim nation [in submission] to You﴾ [al-Baqarah: 128]. So God, Exalted is He, answered him and made them the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ). It is also narrated that he, peace and blessings be upon him, informed that God, Exalted is He, would send Muhammad with the like of his religion, and that his nation would be named "the Muslims." The second is that the pronoun refers to God, Exalted is He, in His saying: ﴿He has chosen you﴾. Atta' narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that he said: "God named you Muslims before," i.e., in all the books, "and in this," i.e., in the Qur'an. This interpretation is closer, because He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿that the Messenger may be a witness over you and that you may be witnesses over the people﴾. So He made clear that He named them with this for this purpose, and this befits none but God. It is also supported by the recitation of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "God named you." The meaning is that He, glorified is He, [named you so] in the books that preceded the Qur'an, and in the Qur'an He also made clear your virtue over the nations and named you with this most noble name, for the sake of the testimony mentioned. So just as God has singled you out with this honour, worship Him and do not reject His obligations. This is the third reason (al-'illah al-thalithah) requiring acceptance of the obligation. As for the discussion of how the Messenger can be a witness over us and how his nation can be witnesses over the people, it has preceded in Surat al-Baqarah, and we explained there that from it is derived what indicates that consensus (ijma') is a proof.

The fourth type: explanation of what serves as a confirmation of what has passed, and it is His saying: ﴿So establish prayer and give zakah﴾
Page 66
It must be understood as referring to the obligatory acts, because they are the well-known ones. ﴿And hold fast to God﴾, i.e., to His rational and transmitted proofs, His kindnesses and His protection. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Ask God for protection from all that is forbidden." al-Qaffal said: Make God a safeguard for you against what you fear. ﴿He is your Protector (mawla)﴾, your Master and the one who disposes over you, ﴿so what an excellent Protector and what an excellent Helper﴾. It is as if He, glorified is He, said: I am your Protector, indeed I am your Helper and sufficient for you. Know that the Mu'tazilah argued with these verses in several ways.

The first: His saying: ﴿that you may be witnesses over the people﴾ indicates that He, glorified is He, intended faith from all. For He does not make a witness over His servants except one who is just and approved. So when He wills that you be witnesses over the people, He has willed that you all be righteous and just, and we know that among them are wrongdoers (fussaq). This indicates that God, Exalted is He, willed for the wrongdoer that he be just.

The second: His saying: ﴿and hold fast to God﴾. How is it possible to hold fast to Him when evil exists only from Him?

The third: His saying: ﴿what an excellent Protector﴾. For if it were as the People of the Sunnah say, that He created most of His servants in order to create disbelief and corruption in them and then punish them, He would not be an excellent Protector; rather, there would be no wicked master except that he is better than Him. So He would have to be described as "a wretched Protector," and that is false. This indicates that He, glorified is He, willed for all of them only righteousness. If it is said: Why could it not be that He is an excellent Protector only for the believers, just as He is an excellent Helper only for them? We say: He, Exalted is He, is the Protector of both believers and disbelievers together, so it must be said that He is an excellent Protector for the believers and a wretched Protector for the disbelievers. If they commit this, they have rejected the Qur'an and the consensus and openly insulted God, Exalted is He.

The fourth: His saying: ﴿He named you Muslims before﴾ indicates the establishment of sharia names, and that they come from God, Exalted is He; for if they were linguistic, they would not be attributed to God, Exalted is He, in a specific way.

The answer to the first: God's being willing for it to be the case that He makes [them] witnesses entails that He is willing for them to be just. So we say: If the willing of a thing entails the willing of its necessary consequences, then the willing of faith from the disbeliever necessitates that it entail willing the ignorance of God, Exalted is He, and so it follows that He, Exalted is He, wills the ignorance of Himself. And if that is not necessary, the argument falls.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿and hold fast to God﴾, it is said: this too applies to you, for He, glorified is He, created desire in the heart of the wrongdoer and reinforced it, created the object of desire and brought it near him, removed the obstacle, then gave the devils of mankind and jinn power over him, and He knew that he would inevitably fall into wickedness and error. In the case of the witness, whoever does this would be a wretched protector. So if the analogy of the absent to the witnessed is valid, this is binding upon you; and if it is invalid, your argument falls entirely.

"The commentary on Surat al-Hajj is complete, and it is followed by the commentary on Surat al-Mu'minun, and all praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds."
